articles.title: PHP2Shell: Your Code Was Fine, The Engine Was Not
articles.description: Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for...
articles.body_html:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

Imagine you do everything right.

You validate your inputs. You use prepared statements. You escape your output. You have a linter, a code review process, and a slightly smug Slack channel called #security-wins.

Then someone sends your server one weird HTTP request, and it runs their code instead of yours.

Not because of anything you wrote.

Because of something PHP did while cleaning up after itself.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project shipped a security release for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The internet has already nicknamed the pair PHP2Shell, which is a great name and a terrible Wednesday.

Let's walk through what actually broke, why it is a bigger deal than "yet another CVE", and also where the scary headlines are a little ahead of the facts.

Why this one is different

PHP is not a niche language. W3Techs says 69.3% of websites whose server-side language it can identify run PHP.

WordPress, Laravel, Drupal, Magento, that one invoice portal from 2014 that nobody dares touch.

Most PHP vulnerabilities live in an application or a plugin. You patch the plugin, you move on.

These two live in the engine.

The engine is the thing underneath your code. It is the C program that parses your PHP, allocates your memory, and tears down after every request.

You can write the most boring, correct PHP of your life, and the floor below it can still have a hole in it.

[DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER] the stack, bottom to top: the web server (Apache or nginx), the SAPI (mod_php or PHP-FPM), the PHP engine, then your application code on top. Highlight the engine layer in red with the caption "both bugs live here, below everything you wrote". Show that an attacker's request has to pass through the engine before your code even sees it.

Both bugs are about the same unglamorous thing: memory management around a request that goes wrong.

To see why, you need to know how PHP spends its life.

PHP's life is one request long

PHP's model is famously "shared nothing".

A request comes in, PHP sets up a fresh little world for it, runs your script, then throws the whole world away.

The worker process survives, but the request's state is supposed to die with the request.

That is why PHP is so forgiving. Leak some memory in a script? Nobody cares, the request ends and the memory gets reclaimed.

Here is the happy path:

flowchart LR
    A([Request arrives]):::start --> B[Request startup<br/>build per-request state]:::engine
    B --> C[Run your script]:::app
    C --> D[Request shutdown<br/>cleanup and free]:::engine
    D --> E([Worker waits for the next request]):::start
    E --> A

    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef engine fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef app fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Notice that the purple boxes, startup and shutdown, are the engine's job.

Your code only owns the teal one in the middle.

Both vulnerabilities are about what happens when something goes wrong between those purple boxes, and the engine's cleanup code assumes a state that no longer holds.

PHP has a hard ceiling on how much memory one request may use, memory_limit. Hit it, and PHP gives up on the request on the spot.

"Gives up on the spot" is where the trouble starts.

Bug 1: cleaning up a house that was never built

CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory one.

Here is the scenario, paraphrasing the PHP Foundation's write-up and Rapid7's analysis.

PHP is in the middle of request startup. It is building that per-request state, piece by piece.

A memory allocation fails. PHP abandons the request abruptly.

But the state is only half built. Some fields are set, some are whatever bytes happened to be sitting in that memory.

Then the cleanup code runs, and it does what cleanup code does: it trusts the state it is handed.

It follows pointers that were never initialized. It frees things that were never allocated. It treats garbage as a structure.

The mental model I like: a demolition crew is sent to tear down a building.

The building was never finished, and the blueprint is a napkin with random scribbles on it.

The crew follows the napkin anyway, and demolishes whatever the scribbles point at.

Here is the shape of the bug as a deliberately simplified sketch. This is not PHP's real source, just the pattern:

// simplified illustration of the bug class, not actual PHP code
int request_startup(request *r) {
    r->headers = alloc_table();     // ok
    r->uploads = alloc_table();     // out of memory! bail out...
    if (!r->uploads) return FAILURE;
    r->hooks   = alloc_table();     // never reached, r->hooks is junk
    return SUCCESS;
}

void request_shutdown(request *r) {
    free_table(r->headers);
    free_table(r->uploads);
    free_table(r->hooks);           // frees a pointer nobody ever set
}

The mistake is not in either function alone. It is in the assumption that shutdown only ever runs on a fully started request.

Now here is the part that makes this one nasty.

How do you make a server run out of memory on purpose? You do not need to hack anything, you just ask nicely and badly.

Rapid7 notes that crafted multipart requests can exhaust memory even when their overall size looks like it fits inside the configured limits.

And on Apache with mod_php, the demonstrated attack happens before any of your application code runs.

That is the whole reason the "zero authentication" line is true. There is no login to bypass. Your code never got the chance to say no.

Memory corruption you can trigger with a request, in a place your app cannot guard, is how you end up with "9.2 critical" in a headline.

Bug 2: the ghost of requests past

CVE-2026-109619, the stale state one.

Same family, different flavour.

Remember that a worker process handles request after request. Some bookkeeping state is global to the worker, and is supposed to be reset between requests.

Now picture this sequence:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Request A
    participant W as PHP worker
    participant B as Request B
    A->>W: runs, global state points at memory M
    W->>W: fatal error interrupts cleanup
    W-->>W: M is freed, but the pointer to M is not cleared
    B->>W: arrives on the same worker
    W->>W: reads the old pointer before init resets it
    Note over W: use-after-free: B is reading memory it does not own

A fatal error, like running out of memory or a timeout, can interrupt the cleanup in the middle.

The memory gets freed, but a pointer to it survives. The next request lands on the same worker, and something reads that pointer before normal initialization has a chance to wipe it.

That is a classic use-after-free. The name is the best part, because the thing you are using after it is free is not free at all, it is very expensive.

Think of a hotel room that was demolished but the key card still opens the door.

Whoever is standing there next gets to decide what is inside.

Rapid7 describes two concrete paths to reach it.

One is the PHP 8.5 fatal error backtrace feature, which is on by default and was confirmed on mod_php. The other is a session upload progress path that works on PHP-FPM, and needs an application operation to leave state behind first.

Note the pattern. Neither bug is about a missing bounds check in some parser. They are both about error paths.

The happy path of PHP has been tested for decades. The path where a request dies at the worst possible moment is the one that gets less love.

So can anyone hack 70% of the internet?

Short answer: no, and it is worth being precise, because the headline version of this story sells more than it delivers.

What is solid:

Both bugs are real and rated 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). Both can lead to code execution as the web worker's user, with no authentication.

RCE was demonstrated by researchers, against real setups, not just crashes.

mod_php is the highest risk. Rapid7 notes that for the OOM bug, mod_php runs cleanup even when startup failed. PHP-FPM kills the worker when startup fails, which blocks that specific sequence.

What is more nuanced:

"Any PHP server" is too strong. Rapid7 reviewed multiple public proof of concepts, and each one works only for a specific combination of OS, PHP version and web server. None is broadly reliable yet.

The attack complexity is rated High. Memory corruption exploits are fiddly. That is a speed bump, not a wall.

Reports of exploitation are mixed. watchTowr says it has seen exploitation in the wild through its honeypots, while Rapid7 has seen attempts but not confirmed in-the-wild compromise.

Whichever way that lands, Rapid7 also warns that a more portable technique could show up quickly.

And the exposed surface is not small. Palo Alto's Unit 42 brief cites telemetry that counts over 22 million potentially vulnerable internet-facing instances. That is a vendor number, so season to taste, but it is the right order of magnitude for "a lot".

If I had to summarize it: not the end of the web, but also not a drill.

The part that is actually uncomfortable

Here is the story behind the patch, and it is the most human part of the whole thing.

flowchart LR
    A[2024<br/>Quarkslab audit,<br/>first signs of the OOM issue]:::early --> B[Fix stalls<br/>competing patches,<br/>each with trade-offs]:::slow
    B --> C[Aug 2026<br/>Calif, OpenAI and Wiz<br/>report it, RCE shown]:::report
    C --> D[Oct 20<br/>CVE IDs leak<br/>2 days early]:::bad
    D --> E[Oct 21<br/>Chainguard images<br/>break the embargo]:::bad
    E --> F[Oct 21, 14:00 UTC<br/>patched releases ship]:::good

    classDef early fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef slow fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef report fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Per the PHP Foundation, an external audit by Quarkslab back in 2024 led a core developer to spot the first signs of the OOM problem while fixing something else.

No exploit path was known at the time.

Then the fix stalled. Competing patches each had a cost: breaking compatibility, opening new denial of service angles, or touching lots of third-party extensions.

The Foundation's own words are refreshingly blunt: the delay was "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."

Then in August 2026 the bug was reported again, with a working unconditional RCE. The CVE IDs leaked online before the release. The embargo then cracked a second time when a vendor published images that already contained the fix.

I find this oddly reassuring and deeply annoying at the same time.

Reassuring, because an open source project wrote that sentence about itself in public, and is changing its process: majority decisions, an ecosystem security team, more staff.

Annoying, because "everyone who maintains critical infrastructure is under-resourced" is not a new lesson, and PHP is carrying a very large share of the web on it.

The AI angle, and where I would push back

A lot of the commentary around this release points at one thing: AI changes who can exploit this.

The argument goes like this. Turning a subtle memory corruption bug into a working attack used to need rare skills. Now somebody with a laptop and an open-weights model can point an agent at the internet, hand it the advisory and say "go find the ones that are still vulnerable".

I think the direction is right and the details are overstated.

What is right: the cost of going from advisory to attempt is falling fast. The patch itself is a diff. A diff tells a model exactly where to look. And scanning is cheap when the scanner does not get tired.

What is overstated: the hard part of this bug is not finding targets, it is the exploit reliability. Rapid7 says the public PoCs are fragile. Memory corruption is a craft, and models are not magic yet at crafting heap layouts for your particular distro.

And there is a side of the story that gets less airtime: the defenders have the same tools.

The Foundation says it used AI-assisted scanning and validation as part of its security work, with the line that "a person makes every call and works on every patch."

So the realistic summary is not "attackers got superpowers". It is this:

The window between "patch published" and "someone is trying it on your server" is shrinking.

Your patching speed is now a security control, not an IT chore.

What to do about it

Boring answer first: update.

The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

If you are on 8.1 or older, there are no routine upstream releases. Rapid7 notes limited source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, so lean on your distribution or an LTS vendor, or finally take the upgrade you have been postponing since 2022.

Two gotchas people will trip on:

A patched package on disk is not a patched process in memory. Running workers keep the old code until they restart. Qualys specifically calls this out, so restart or gracefully reload your PHP services after upgrading.

Containers do not save you from stale base images. If your image was built last week, it is still carrying last week's PHP.

Quick check:

php -v                       # compare against 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35

# then make sure the running workers are the new ones
sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm     # or: apachectl graceful

If you truly cannot patch yet, the advisories list temporary mitigations. They reduce exposure, they do not fix it:

; php.ini or FPM pool config, NOT ini_set() or .user.ini (too late for these)
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0   ; closes the known session path
fatal_error_backtraces = 0            ; PHP 8.5 only
post_max_size = 8M                    ; and cap multipart size at the frontend too

You will see memory_limit=-1 suggested too, and here is where I have to confess the Roll Safe meme is doing real work:

It genuinely appears in the advisory guidance, set administratively so apps cannot override it. But Rapid7 is clear that an allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path, so it narrows the window and does not close it.

Also, a server with no memory limit has its own personality. It is called "an outage".

And two things not to reach for. Rapid7 warns that RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA can themselves trigger the vulnerable allocation failure path, and container or cgroup memory limits are an incomplete answer and can kill the whole worker pool.

Do not hide the evidence either. Silencing errors with display_errors or @ does not prevent stale state from being read, and a quiet log is not proof you are fine.

Here is the whole decision as a flowchart, for the person who has a patch window and a manager:

flowchart TD
    A([Do you run PHP on a web server?]):::start --> B{Is it on 8.2.35, 8.3.36,<br/>8.4.27 or 8.5.12 or newer?}:::decision
    B -- yes --> C{Did you restart or reload<br/>workers after upgrading?}:::decision
    C -- yes --> D([You are patched. Go touch grass.]):::good
    C -- no --> E[Restart workers now]:::action
    B -- no --> F{Is it 8.1 or older?}:::decision
    F -- yes --> G[Distro or LTS backport,<br/>or plan the upgrade]:::action
    F -- no --> H[Upgrade to a fixed release]:::action
    G --> I[Apply interim mitigations<br/>until it lands]:::warn
    H --> E

    classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef action fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef warn fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a

The thing worth taking away

The patch is the urgent lesson. The durable one is quieter.

Your security posture includes layers you did not write and never read.

Your code can be perfect and the runtime under it can still ship a bug that was first noticed two years ago.

That is not a reason to panic about PHP specifically. Every runtime has error paths nobody loves, and the next bug of this kind will be in a different one.

It is a reason to treat runtime and base image updates as first class work, to know which version is actually running in production, and to keep the gap between "advisory" and "deployed" as small as you can.

Cleanup code, it turns out, is also code.

Maybe even the code most worth reviewing.

I was building a social media platform named Crowdwide!

It has this special thing about it... it helps the newer voices get discovered. Its algorithm is designed like that!!

So... for the newer voices and higher engagement, I just integrated Widewave, and I was not expecting it to get indexed on Google within 24 hours! 😭

More than 5 posts are getting indexed, and others will be there soon... lol.

That increases the reach of the platform and the posts of new voices.

So, I think all the algorithms, user engagement emails, notifications, and main features are almost done.

I think I just need a little UI improvement now! And then 2–3 days of testing!

And in UI improvements, I need to fix the sidebars, and a few buttons are very close to each other. I need to fix those, and... all set!

Finally, I feel like I'm at the moment where it's just done!

But idk how this just goes on. I need to add this... just this much, this much more... hmm... more and more...

But I think this is enough. I just need UI improvements now, and that's it for now!

Further, I got 12 users now, and 60 posts on Crowdwide are completed. Ik most of them are devlogs, but still, I count this as part of building, too. I also posted my old artwork there—a paper flower built by me:

https://www.crowdwide.run.place/posts/6ad739d24eabf9bab7720410

I will post things on it... some interesting things, and maybe on different topics...

I don't want its feed to get dead!

And the number of communities is still the same!

There's no major growth in the number of users. I found mostly old users there.

So, I will try to make a few more posts on different topics and try to continue until it gets its first 100 users.

Ik it may take a lot of time, but I will try this.

articles.title: The Hidden Bugs Behind Duplicate API Requests
articles.description: One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical...
articles.body_html:
One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical down to the last field.

Nothing in the frontend code looks wrong. The server logs show two requests, both returning 201. Whoever wrote the endpoint is fairly sure it only creates one order per call, and they're right. It was called twice.

"Duplicate request" is a symptom with at least six different causes, and the fixes don't overlap much. Some of these causes are harmless (React in development), some are annoying (a double-clicked button), and one is genuinely dangerous: a client that timed out and sent the request again, while the server had already done the work. This article goes through them roughly in the order I'd check them, and spends the most time on that last one, because it's the one that costs money.

Before you debug: is it really a duplicate?

Three things look like duplicates and aren't.

CORS preflight. A cross-origin request with a JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a method like PUT makes the browser send an OPTIONS request first. In DevTools the URL appears twice. Look at the Method column. (MDN: CORS preflight)

Development-only behavior. If the doubles show up on your machine but not in production, go straight to the React section below.

A different caller. A service worker, browser extension, or second tab can send requests that resemble yours. The Initiator column in the Network tab points at the line that started each request.

Then do the single most useful thing: log a request ID on the server. One request on the server means you're misreading the client. Two means keep reading.

React runs your effect twice (on purpose) 

function Product({ id }) {
  const [product, setProduct] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/products/${id}`)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setProduct);
  }, [id]);
}

Under <StrictMode> in development, this sends two requests on mount. In a production build it sends one.

That's deliberate. With Strict Mode on, React runs an extra setup, cleanup, setup cycle on each effect in development, to expose effects that don't clean up after themselves. The behavior arrived with React 18, and the surprise it caused is well documented in facebook/react #24502, where users asked for it to be explained better in the docs.

Removing Strict Mode makes the symptom disappear and leaves the bug. If an effect misbehaves when it runs twice, it will also misbehave when a user navigates away and back.

For reads, add a cleanup that cancels the request:

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/products/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setProduct)
    .catch(err => {
      if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err);
    });

  return () => controller.abort();
}, [id]);

You'll still see two requests in the Network tab in development, but the first is cancelled and only the second can touch state. An AbortController is better than the common ignore flag here: as this DEV Community post points out, the flag discards the result but still lets the first request download its whole response.

Cancelling on the client does not undo anything the server already did. Which brings up the real question this section raises: what is the effect doing? A duplicate GET is noise. A duplicate POST fired from an effect means a non-idempotent action is tied to rendering. React's guidance is that effects exist to synchronize with external systems, and that you don't need an effect to handle a user event. Creating an order belongs in the click handler, where it runs once per click.

Race conditions: the stale response wins

Sometimes two different requests are in flight and the older one finishes last.

A search box fires on every keystroke. The user types "re", then "react". The request for "re" is slow, the one for "react" is quick. Results for "react" render, then results for "re" arrive and overwrite them. The page now shows results for a query that no longer matches the input.

Nothing was sent twice, and nothing here is React-specific. The UI depends on the order responses arrive instead of the order the user acted. The cleanup shown above fixes it, since React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect. If you'd rather not cancel, the flag version works too:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(data => { if (!ignore) setResults(data); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [query]);

Debouncing the input reduces how many requests you send. The cleanup makes sure the right one wins. They solve different problems, and a search box usually needs both.

The double click

A checkout button, an 800 ms API call, and a user who isn't sure the first click registered.

Disabling the button during submission is the obvious fix, with one catch. State updates don't apply synchronously inside the handler that sets them, so two clicks that land before React re-renders can both pass an if (submitting) check. A ref closes that gap:

function CheckoutButton() {
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const inFlight = useRef(false);

  async function handleClick() {
    if (inFlight.current) return;   // the real lock
    inFlight.current = true;
    setSubmitting(true);            // the visual feedback
    try {
      await placeOrder();
    } finally {
      inFlight.current = false;
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick} disabled={submitting}>
      {submitting ? 'Placing order…' : 'Place order'}
    </button>
  );
}

This protects one component in one tab. A second tab, a mobile app, or a retry after a dropped connection walks right past it. Treat it as UI feedback, and keep the safety check on the server.

The same handler attached twice

If the server log shows two identical requests a few milliseconds apart and the button logic is fine, count the listeners.

// runs on every route change
function init() {
  document.querySelector('#save')
    .addEventListener('click', () => saveDraft());
}

addEventListener ignores a repeat registration only when the function reference and capture flag are the same. An inline arrow function is a new object every call, so after three route changes one click runs saveDraft() three times. (MDN: addEventListener)

The usual sources are SPA code that attaches listeners imperatively on every navigation, jQuery's .on() inside a function that runs on every partial render, and React effects that subscribe without returning a cleanup. A form with both onSubmit on the <form> and onClick on its submit button doing the same job produces the same symptom.

In Chrome DevTools, select the element and open the Event Listeners panel. Two click entries where you expected one is your answer.

Retries: duplicates made by code that's trying to help

This is the case worth slowing down for.

You send a POST /orders. Ten seconds pass. Your client times out. Here is everything you know at that moment: you did not receive a response. Here is what you don't know:

  1. The request never reached the server.
  2. The server processed it, and the response was lost on the way back.
  3. The server is still working on it.

From the client these three look identical. If you retry in case 2 or 3, the operation runs twice.

HTTP has vocabulary for this. RFC 9110, section 9.2.2 defines idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE, where repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. POST isn't in that set, and neither is PATCH in general. The RFC's error-handling section also notes that some requests can be automatically retried after a connection failure, pointing to section 9.2.2 for which ones. Secondary write-ups summarize the rule as: don't automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless you know it's effectively idempotent or can tell the original was never applied (ApyHub, a DEV Community post on safe failover).

Check what your client library does by default

Retry behavior varies by library and version, so read your client's documentation instead of assuming. One public example: a GitLab client-library change (merge request 2945) added an option to restrict retries to idempotent methods, because its default check retried any method on a 5xx response, which could duplicate a side effect the server had already applied. That's one project's default, but it shows how the problem hides: nobody wrote a retry for POST /orders; a generic retry policy did.

Retries multiply across layers

If the browser code retries 3 times, the API gateway retries 3 times, and the service retries its database call 3 times, one click can become 27 attempts at the bottom. Amazon's Builders' Library article on timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter makes this point about stacked retries, and also calls retries "selfish": each one spends more of the server's time to improve the caller's odds. Its recommendations are timeouts based on downstream latency, capped exponential backoff, jitter so clients don't all retry in lockstep, and limiting retries (the AWS SDK has used a token bucket for this since 2016).

Infrastructure retries too. Reverse proxies can pass a failed request to another upstream. For example, nginx's proxy_next_upstream documents that non-idempotent requests aren't passed on by default unless you opt in with non_idempotent. Read the equivalent setting for whatever sits in front of your app, and check access logs on every hop.

A retry helper that actually retries HTTP failures

One trap when writing your own: fetch() resolves successfully even when the server answers 503. A try/catch around it never sees the failure. You have to look at the status yourself.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(res) {
    super(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    this.status = res.status;
  }
}

const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') return false;
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(err.status);
  return err instanceof TypeError; // fetch rejects with TypeError on network failure
}

async function withRetry(fn, { retries = 4, baseMs = 200, capMs = 5000 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
      const delay = Math.random() * ceiling;          // full jitter
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
}

// usage
const res = await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', { method: 'POST', /* ... */ });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

I ran this helper against a stub that returns 503 twice and then 201: it made three attempts and returned the 201. A 400 was thrown after one attempt, as intended. A production version should also honor a Retry-After header when the server sends one.

Retrying a POST with this helper is only safe if the server can recognize the repeat. That's the next section.

Making the server safe to call twice

Everything above reduces how often a duplicate arrives. None of it can remove the three-way ambiguity after a timeout, because the network is allowed to lose a response. For operations that must not happen twice, the main defense is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation, the server records it with the result, and a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

Stripe's API is the best-known example. Their documentation says the idempotency layer saves the status code and body of the first request for a key, whether it succeeded or failed, and returns that for later requests with the same key. Keys can be up to 255 characters, and reusing a key with different parameters produces an error. GET and DELETE don't take keys because they're idempotent by definition.

There's also a standards effort: the IETF HTTPAPI working group's Idempotency-Key HTTP header field draft. As of the version I read (draft-07, October 2025), it's an active Internet-Draft, not an RFC, so details may change.

Client: create the key once, reuse it on every retry 

// Create it when the user's intent is created (page load, checkout start),
// never inside the retry loop.
const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(order),
  });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

A new key per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Server: let the database arbitrate

The sketch below uses Express and PostgreSQL. It's an illustration of the pattern: I haven't run the SQL against a live database, so test it in your own stack, including the concurrent case.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key           text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  text NOT NULL,
  response_code int  NOT NULL,
  response_body jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

// Same payload in a different key order must hash the same.
function canonicalize(v) {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return v.map(canonicalize);
  if (v && typeof v === 'object') {
    return Object.fromEntries(
      Object.keys(v).sort().map(k => [k, canonicalize(v[k])])
    );
  }
  return v;
}

app.post('/api/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get('Idempotency-Key');
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key required' });

  const hash = sha256(JSON.stringify(canonicalize(req.body)));
  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    // Claim the key. The PRIMARY KEY decides who wins a race.
    const claim = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash, response_code, response_body)
       VALUES ($1, $2, 0, '{}')
       ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING key`,
      [key, hash]
    );

    if (claim.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      const { rows: [saved] } = await pool.query(
        'SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = $1',
        [key]
      );
      if (!saved) return res.status(409).set('Retry-After', '1').end(); // first attempt rolled back
      if (saved.request_hash !== hash) {
        return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Key reused with a different payload' });
      }
      return res.status(saved.response_code).json(saved.response_body);
    }

    // We own the key. Do the work, in the same transaction.
    const order = await createOrder(client, req.body);
    const body = { id: order.id };

    await client.query(
      `UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response_code = 201, response_body = $2 WHERE key = $1`,
      [key, body]
    );
    await client.query('COMMIT');
    return res.status(201).json(body);
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => {});
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

Three design points are worth spelling out.

Why INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and not "check, then insert." A SELECT followed by an INSERT has a gap, and two simultaneous requests can both pass the check. Letting a unique constraint decide closes the gap. As I understand PostgreSQL's behavior, a second insert of the same key blocks until the first transaction commits or rolls back, which is why the example doesn't need an in_progress state. Verify that against your isolation level and driver.

Why one transaction. Creating the order and recording the key together means a crash can't leave an order without a key, or a key without an order. This only works when both writes live in the same database. Once the operation involves something outside that transaction (a payment provider, a message queue, an email), the guarantee stops at the transaction boundary. For those, pass a key derived from yours to the provider's own idempotency mechanism, and consider an explicit in_progress state with a defined policy for concurrent callers, such as 409 with Retry-After.

Why canonicalize before hashing. JSON.stringify preserves key order, so {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} hash differently even though they mean the same thing. Without canonicalization, a legitimate retry from a different serializer gets rejected as "key reused with a different payload."

When a simpler rule is enough

If the domain gives you natural uniqueness, such as one open order per (user_id, cart_id), a unique constraint can reject the duplicate without any key table. Idempotency keys are the more general tool, and constraints are the cheaper one when they fit.

Idempotency isn't the only defense either. Uniqueness constraints, transactional design and operation-specific checks all contribute. What an idempotency key gives you that they don't is a consistent answer to the retry: the same response, not an error saying "already exists."

A checklist for the next time you see doubles

  1. Is one of them an OPTIONS preflight?
  2. Does it happen in a production build? If not, check Strict Mode and effect cleanups.
  3. What does the Initiator column say about each request?
  4. How many listeners does the element have?
  5. Does the server log show one request or two? Log a request ID.
  6. Are the two requests identical, or do query strings differ? Different ones suggest a race or dependency-array bug, not a retry.
  7. How far apart are the timestamps? Milliseconds points at a double-click or double-mount. Seconds points at a timeout and retry.
  8. Which layers retry? Browser code, client library, gateway, load balancer, service client, job queue.
  9. Can this endpoint safely run twice? If not, fix that first.

The first eight steps tell you why a duplicate happened. The ninth decides whether it matters.

articles.title: PHP2Shell, explained: the two critical PHP bugs every team needs to patch
articles.description: On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in...
articles.body_html:
On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself. The pair is being called PHP2Shell:

  • CVE-2026-109618
  • CVE-2026-109619

Both have a 9.2 Critical CVSS score. Both can expose vulnerable PHP services to unauthenticated remote code execution and memory disclosure. And neither one is fixed by updating Laravel, WordPress, Symfony, a Composer package, or your application code.

This is the important part:

The vulnerable thing is the PHP interpreter that runs your application.

So yes, the meme is funny. The patch window is not.

First: should you be worried?

You should move this to the top of the queue if you run PHP on an internet-facing service and your runtime is any version from PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

That includes more than the obvious php-fpm server in a VM:

  • PHP-FPM behind Nginx or Apache
  • Apache mod_php
  • WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Moodle, and other PHP-based products
  • Docker images built from php:* base images
  • Kubernetes workloads
  • queue workers and scheduled jobs
  • application images deployed to Cloud Run, ECS, App Engine Flexible, or similar platforms
  • vendor software that silently bundles its own PHP runtime

This is why security incidents around language runtimes are awkward: everyone knows where the repository is, but fewer teams can answer which PHP binary is actually serving production traffic right now?

What actually happened?

PHP receives a request, allocates memory, builds internal structures, runs your code, cleans everything up, and does it again for the next request. Most of the time, none of this is visible to an application developer. It should not be visible.

PHP2Shell lives in the parts of that lifecycle you only notice when something has already gone wrong: out-of-memory handling, cleanup, freed memory, and reused workers.

Think of a restaurant kitchen.

Normally, an order comes in, a tray is prepared, food is served, the tray is cleaned, and the next order starts with an empty tray. These vulnerabilities are different flavours of the kitchen being interrupted mid-cleanup—and the next order being served from a tray the system thought was safe, but was not.

That is a deliberately simplified analogy. The practical consequence is not: “your page crashes.” The reported impact is much worse: an unauthenticated attacker may be able to manipulate the runtime into leaking memory or executing code in the PHP process.

The two CVEs, in human language

CVE The technical shape The plain-English version Why defenders care
CVE-2026-109618 During an out-of-memory condition, PHP can be interrupted while request data is only partially initialized. Subsequent cleanup can treat that invalid state as valid. The runtime gets interrupted while setting up the request, then later cleans up a half-built object as if it were complete. The failure path can become an attacker-controlled path.
CVE-2026-109619 Request-owned state can remain reachable after its backing memory has been freed. A later request on the same worker can use stale state before normal initialization resets it. One request leaves behind a poisonous sticky note; the next request on the same worker reads it before the desk is reset. Long-lived, reused PHP workers make cross-request state especially relevant.

The research and vendor advisories use precise memory-management language because the details matter for exploitability. You do not need to reproduce that research to respond safely. The operational conclusion is already clear: update the runtime, restart/redeploy every worker that might still have the old binary or old in-memory state, and verify the version that is actually live.

Why “we use a framework” is not the answer

Framework updates are valuable. They just solve a different class of problem.

A typical framework vulnerability might be triggered by a route, a package feature, an insecure deserialization path, or an app-level configuration choice. With PHP2Shell, the issue is underneath that stack:

Your application
↓
Laravel / WordPress / Symfony / custom code
↓
Composer dependencies
↓
PHP runtime   ← the vulnerable layer
↓
OS or container image

You can have pristine dependencies, a clean SAST report, and still be running an affected PHP interpreter. That is why the right opening question is not “Which repo uses PHP?” It is “Which live workloads execute PHP?”

Which versions are affected—and what fixes them?

The disclosed affected range is PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

The initial fixed upstream releases are:

Supported branch Fixed release
PHP 8.5 8.5.12
PHP 8.4 8.4.27
PHP 8.3 8.3.36
PHP 8.2 8.2.35

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and are not receiving an upstream fix. If you are on one of those branches, the decision is not “which patch do we wait for?” It is “which supported PHP branch can we upgrade to safely and quickly?”

One nuance for distro users: a Linux distribution can backport a security patch while retaining a different-looking upstream version string. Follow your distribution’s security advisory and package changelog, then verify the installed package. For custom builds and official PHP images, move to a fixed upstream release.

The container trap: patching the host may change nothing

This is the moment where many incident checklists quietly fail.

Imagine a host running the latest system PHP package. Great. But your production app is deployed as this:

FROM php:8.3-fpm
COPY . /var/www/html

The PHP process serving requests came from the image, not from the host package manager. Updating the host does not alter the PHP binary already baked into that image.

The real fix path is:

update base image or PHP package
→ rebuild image
→ push a new immutable digest
→ redeploy every workload
→ verify the running container

The same rule applies to queue workers, cron jobs, admin jobs, and one-off worker deployments. They often have a separate Dockerfile, release pipeline, or autoscaling pool.

“The build succeeded” is not the final check. “The running workload uses the patched runtime” is.

A calm, practical response plan

1. Find every runtime

Start by checking what a machine or container is running:

php -v
php --ini

For container fleets, find images that contain PHP, then inspect the deployed digest in your orchestration platform. Search your CI definitions too: the old base image may be pinned in a reusable workflow rather than in the application repository.

Do not forget:

  • background queues
  • scheduled jobs
  • worker pools
  • maintenance scripts
  • staging and pre-production environments that hold production-like data
  • marketplace or vendor products with bundled PHP

2. Patch the runtime

Update to the fixed release for your supported branch—or to a vendor-confirmed package that contains the backported fix. For source builds, use the fixed upstream release. For containers, rebuild from a fixed base image or package set.

3. Restart or redeploy the processes

Installing a package is only half a fix if PHP-FPM or Apache is still running an old process in memory. Restart the relevant service. In container platforms, deploy fresh tasks/pods/instances from the patched image.

This matters especially for a bug involving request-owned state and reused workers: stale, running processes are not where you want to gamble on “probably fine.”

4. Verify the live environment

Check the runtime version from a newly started process, not just from your laptop or CI log:

php -v

For containers, also verify the new image digest is the one your deployment actually pulled. An autoscaler can keep old replicas alive longer than expected; an image tag can be reused; a rollout can partially fail. Those are normal operational problems. They are also how a completed patch turns into an incomplete remediation.

5. Monitor and investigate, without turning this into panic theatre

The FBI’s public guidance recommends prioritizing internet-facing systems, watching for suspicious PHP processes launching command shells or downloading files, and preserving relevant logs if compromise indicators appear. Qualys also reported that Cloudflare had observed attack traffic, which is a good reason to treat external exposure as urgent rather than theoretical.

Useful places to review:

  • web-server access and error logs
  • PHP-FPM / Apache error logs
  • process-execution telemetry from affected hosts and containers
  • WAF and load-balancer events
  • application error-rate and restart telemetry
  • image-scanner results after the rebuild

Unexpected 5xx spikes, repeated process crashes, large unusual request bodies, unexpected shell processes, or unexplained downloads deserve incident-response attention. They are signals to investigate—not proof by themselves that the CVE was exploited.

“Can a WAF save us?”

A WAF can buy time. It cannot patch a vulnerable interpreter.

Cloud guidance for this incident recommends using managed WAF protections and being careful about oversized request bodies while patching. That is reasonable defence in depth, especially for public applications. Roll new rules out in preview/canary mode where feasible, look for application-specific false positives, then enforce them.

But do not let a temporary rule become a reason to defer the update. A rule protects only the traffic it sees, only the shapes it recognizes, and only the applications placed behind it. The runtime update is the remediation.

The posts people are sharing on X

These are real posts published after the disclosure. They are included here because they add useful operational perspective—not because social media is a source of truth. The PHP security advisory and your platform/vendor guidance should drive the actual patch plan.

FBI Cyber Division: treat exposed installations as urgent

Qualys: patch, restart workers, and verify the runtime

Datadog: check versions across the organization

The things teams will get wrong this week

“We updated WordPress, so we are safe.”

Maybe you are safer from a WordPress vulnerability. That is not the same as replacing the PHP binary that runs WordPress.

“We upgraded the server package.”

Excellent—unless the service runs inside a container, an immutable image, a separate worker pool, or a vendor distribution with its own runtime.

“Our scanner says the repository is clean.”

Source scanning does not prove the running infrastructure has the right runtime. Scan the image, check the deployed digest, and verify the live process.

“We are on PHP 8.1, but it is stable.”

Stable is not supported. There is no upstream security release for PHP 8.1 or older here. Upgrade planning just became incident response work.

“We put a WAF rule in front of it.”

Good temporary mitigation. Still not a patch.

Your incident checklist

  • [ ] Identify every production, worker, and scheduled workload that executes PHP.
  • [ ] Confirm whether its PHP runtime is in the affected range.
  • [ ] Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35, or a vendor-confirmed patched build.
  • [ ] Upgrade PHP 8.1 and older to a supported branch.
  • [ ] Rebuild custom images without relying on a stale cache.
  • [ ] Redeploy every workload and restart long-lived PHP processes.
  • [ ] Verify the live runtime version and image digest.
  • [ ] Apply temporary WAF/edge controls while rollout completes.
  • [ ] Review security telemetry and preserve evidence if compromise indicators appear.
  • [ ] Record which environments are verified and which still need work.

The takeaway

PHP is a widely deployed runtime having a serious emergency patch day.

The less funny takeaway is that runtime upgrades cannot live forever in a low-priority maintenance bucket. The moment a core vulnerability lands, the teams that respond well are the ones that already know:

  1. where their runtimes are,
  2. how their images are built,
  3. how to roll out a change everywhere, and
  4. how to prove that the change reached production.

Patch it. Redeploy it. Verify it.

References

  • PHP’s October 21 security announcement
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109618
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109619
  • Google Cloud’s remediation guidance

Have you checked your worker images yet, or only the web servers?

articles.title: PHP2Shell: Check Every Installed PHP Version on Debian 12 and 13
articles.description: A read-only, open-source checker for PHP2Shell fixes across installed PHP packages on Debian 12 and...
articles.body_html:
A read-only, open-source checker for PHP2Shell fixes across installed PHP packages on Debian 12 and 13."

You update PHP, run php -v, and see a patched version.

But which PHP version is actually serving your websites?

A server can have multiple PHP branches installed. Your default CLI binary might be current while a website still uses an older PHP-FPM pool. Checking one version leaves a practical gap.

That is the problem behind PHP2Shell Checker, a small open-source tool I built with Codex while working through the update process for my Debian servers.

Get the code: GitHub · GitLab

PHP2Shell refers to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two PHP vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21, 2026, and recommends updating immediately. The advisory covers web-serving installations including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, CGI, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Official PHP advisory.

For the standard Debian packages, the fixed versions are:

Distribution PHP branch Fixed package version
Debian 12 — bookworm PHP 8.2 8.2.35-1~deb12u1
Debian 13 — trixie PHP 8.4 8.4.27-1~deb13u1

These thresholds are documented in Debian's security advisories: DLA-4848-1 and DSA-6574-1.

The checker brings the relevant package information into one report. It:

  • Inventories recognized PHP core packages across installed branches, including CLI, FPM, CGI, and Apache mod_php.
  • Compares installed versions against known fixed thresholds.
  • Shows the candidate versions available through APT.
  • Identifies held packages that may block updates.
  • Searches common installation directories for PHP runtimes outside the assessed packages.
  • Prints suggested update commands when a newer, verified fixed candidate is available.

It runs locally, uses the Python standard library, and requires no external Python packages. The checker itself makes no network requests and performs no system changes. It does not execute PHP binaries or attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities.

To use it on Debian 12 or 13:

git clone https://github.com/toxy4ny/php2shell-checker.git
cd php2shell-checker

# Refresh APT's package information separately.
sudo apt update

# Run the checker.
python3 check-php2shell.py

Resolve any apt update errors before relying on the candidate versions in the report. The checker reads your local APT indexes.

For an additional PHP installation directory:

python3 check-php2shell.py --scan-root /www/server/php

You will see one of three statuses:

Status What it means
FIXED Package metadata meets a known patched version threshold.
UPDATE A recognizable Debian package version is below its fixed threshold.
UNKNOWN The checker cannot automatically confirm remediation.

Here is an illustrative result:

[UPDATE] php8.2-fpm  installed=8.2.34-1~deb12u1
  Debian package version below 8.2.35-1~deb12u1

UNKNOWN is a deliberate part of the design.

A vendor may backport a security fix without adopting the latest upstream version number. Declaring every older third-party build vulnerable would be misleading. Declaring it fixed without evidence would be worse.

For those cases, the checker asks you to verify the vendor's advisory. Its rules are embedded in the script, dated October 22, 2026; they are not automatically refreshed.

There is another boundary worth understanding: updated packages do not prove that running PHP workers have been restarted. After applying updates, restart the affected PHP-FPM services, Apache when using mod_php, and relevant long-running PHP workers. Then verify your sites.

Containers, chroots, arbitrary custom builds, and application code require separate checks. A FIXED result describes the assessed package metadata; it does not certify the entire server or rule out an earlier compromise.

We tested the checker in Debian 12 and Debian 13 containers, including comparisons using real dpkg, and ran it against installed PHP packages. GitHub Actions also passed for both distributions. The project includes eight automated tests and is available under the MIT license.

If you maintain Debian PHP servers, inspect the script and run it against your installations. Check every PHP runtime that serves traffic, apply the relevant updates, and restart the affected workers.

Contributions are welcome—especially regression tests and additional version rules backed by primary vendor advisories. Please redact sensitive paths and server details when opening issues.

Check your servers with PHP2Shell Checker →

articles.title: I Built an Agent Skill That Tests Your App Like Four First-Time Users
articles.description: Four simulated first-time users, one simple audit workflow, and a copy-paste prompt to try it on your app.
articles.body_html:
When you're building an app, you already know where every button leads and what the user is supposed to do next.

Your first-time visitors don't.

That's why I built First User Audit — an open-source Agent Skill that helps coding agents explore your application from four different first-time-user perspectives.

It focuses on one question:

Can someone reach the first useful result without getting stuck?

Four perspectives, one app

The skill uses four simulated user behaviors:

  • Impatient — Skims the page, clicks the obvious button, and quickly gives up when things get confusing.
  • Skeptic — Checks pricing, privacy, and terms before trusting the product.
  • Mobile — Explores the experience at a 375px viewport.
  • Breaker — Tries invalid inputs, retries, back navigation, and double submissions.

What does the skill actually do?

It guides your coding agent through a simple process:

  1. Identify what first success means for your app.
  2. Explore the onboarding journey through four different behaviors.
  3. Record blockers with browser evidence and reproduction steps.
  4. Prioritize issues and propose safe technical fixes.
  5. Verify changes through fresh sessions when supported.

The idea is to catch friction that can be easy to overlook when you're already familiar with your product.

Try it with your coding agent

You can install it using the skills CLI, or simply copy this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, or another compatible coding agent:

Install the first-user-audit Agent Skill from:
https://github.com/BarganConstantin/agent-skills

Use the skills CLI:
npx skills add BarganConstantin/agent-skills --skill first-user-audit

Verify that the skill is installed.

Inspect my application and identify the first useful
outcome a new user should reach.

If a safe local or isolated preview environment and
browser automation are available, run the four
first-user personas with fresh browser sessions.

Collect evidence, identify friction, propose bounded
technical fixes, and verify changes with fresh
agent contexts when supported.

Do not use production data or live payments.
Ask before sensitive changes or reduced-isolation runs.

If anything is missing, explain how to set it up.
Never invent test results.

The skill requires connected browser tooling for the audit. Independent subagents depend on your coding environment, and simulated personas don't replace real usability testing.

It's open source under the MIT license.

Explore First User Audit on GitHub

Give it a try

If you use it on your own project, I'd love to hear what happens.

Did it catch an issue you hadn't noticed? Did it miss something obvious? Was the setup straightforward?

Share your experience in the comments. Feedback, ideas, and contributions are always welcome.

articles.title: I Let an LLM Art-Direct Lyric Videos. Then I Took Most of the Job Away.
articles.description: I've been building LyricVideoGenerator, a tool that takes a song and its lyrics and renders a lyric...
articles.body_html:
I've been building LyricVideoGenerator, a tool that takes a song and its lyrics and renders a lyric video where each word lights up as it's sung. Most of the people using it make songs with Suno or Udio and want something to post on YouTube that isn't a static cover image.

The pitch is that you don't design anything. You drop in a song and get three finished looks to pick from. Somebody has to make those three looks. My first answer was "the LLM does it," and it didn't survive testing. This post is about what replaced it.

TL;DR: Letting the LLM design the whole look worked, but took up to a minute and kept producing the same three designs. Now the LLM only labels the song (mood, genre, energy, chorus lines), and plain code picks three looks from a library of hand-built presets.

The renderer only reads JSON

The video is a Remotion composition, and the only thing it reads is a Style object:

type Style = {
  template: 'focus' | 'scroll' | 'caption';
  palette: { bg: string; fg: string; accent: string; muted: string };
  typography: { family: string; weight: 400 | 500 | 600 | 700 | 800 | 900;
                scale: number; transform: 'none' | 'uppercase';
                align: 'left' | 'center' };
  background:
    | { kind: 'solid' }
    | { kind: 'gradient'; from: string; to: string; angle: number }
    | { kind: 'cover-blur'; blur: number; dim: number }
    | { kind: 'image'; url: string; dim: number };
  animation: 'word-highlight' | 'karaoke' | 'line-fade'
           | 'word-pop' | 'typewriter';
  sections: { chorus: SectionStyle; verse?: SectionStyle; /* ... */ };
  // plus emphasis words, a cover badge flag, a name and a one-line rationale
};

So "design a lyric video" really means "fill in this object." That made it look like a perfect LLM job: a closed schema, a bounded set of choices, and taste as the only hard part.

Version 1: the model designs everything

The first prompt described what each field does on screen (the focus template shows one line at 110px, caption puts a subtitle block in the lower-left third, and so on) and asked for three complete Style objects per song.

Zod validation alone wasn't enough. Only about 4% of calls failed on structure, but the output was still often unusable. The failures that mattered were about meaning.

  • Fonts that don't exist. Big Shoulders Display showed up twice; Google Fonts merged it into Big Shoulders a while ago. I ended up shipping a list of all 1,950 Google Fonts families and rejecting anything not on it.
  • Highlight you can't see. For cover-based looks it would pull two near-white colours from the album art and use one for the lyrics and one for the highlighted word. On screen you couldn't tell which word was being sung.
  • Half an empty screen. It paired the caption template with a flat colour background. caption exists to leave the top two-thirds of the frame to the cover art, so over a solid colour you get half a screen of nothing. That was 3 of 18 candidates in one round.

Each of those turned into a check: a font allowlist, contrast thresholds (lyrics at least 4.5:1 against whatever is actually behind them, the highlight colour at least 3:1), and "caption only over cover backgrounds." For background images I compute the real colour behind the text with sharp (average and brightest colour of the cover, blended with the overlay at its dim value) instead of trusting the model's bg field.

The rule I held to: code validates and repairs, it never makes visual decisions.

Problem What the code does
Weight the font doesn't ship Snap to the nearest weight it does
Low contrast Heavier overlay first, then shift lightness, keep the hue
Emphasis word at the wrong index (off by one, twice) Look it up again by its text
Anything else Send it back to the model with the error attached

With that in place it worked. Across 6 songs × 3 runs, every run produced 3 valid candidates within one retry, and when I went through the 18 chorus frames, 15 were usable as-is.

Why it still wasn't good enough

Two problems that more validation couldn't fix.

Latency. Three full designs took 40–60 seconds at the median and up to ~100 seconds. The cost was fine (two or three cents per song). Waiting a minute after uploading a song is not.

Sameness. Every song got its own three looks, but across songs the pattern was obvious. Over 54 candidates the template was locked to the slot: the first was always focus, the third always caption. The "bold" option was nearly always a dark gradient, centred heavy type and an amber highlight. Anyone making their third video would notice the AI has three moulds.

I tried prompt work on the second problem. Removing hard-coded suggestions and asking for genre-specific choices raised font variety from 12 families over 18 candidates to 15 or 16, but the template-by-slot pattern never went away.

Version 2: the model tags, code picks

What runs in production now splits the job:

  1. One cheap LLM call reads the lyrics and style tags and returns only labels: 1–3 moods, 1–2 genres, an energy level, which lines are the chorus, and 3–6 emphasis words.
  2. Code scores every hand-built preset against those labels.
  3. Code picks the best set of three under some diversity rules.
  4. Presets marked "from cover" pull their palette from the album art, and everything goes through the same validator as before.

The scoring is deliberately boring. Mood counts most, then genre, then how close the energy level is:

// weighted overlap: the first mood/genre the LLM lists counts most
const hit = (tags: string[], picked: string[], w: number[]) =>
  picked.reduce((s, x, i) => s + (tags.includes(x) ? w[i] : 0), 0) /
  picked.reduce((s, _, i) => s + w[i], 0);

export function scorePreset(p: Preset, a: Analysis) {
  const m = hit(p.tags.mood, a.mood, [1, 0.7, 0.5]);
  const g = hit(p.tags.genre, a.genre, [1, 0.6]);
  const d = Math.abs(ENERGY_ORD[p.tags.energy] - ENERGY_ORD[a.energy]);
  const e = d === 0 ? 1 : d === 1 ? 0.4 : 0;
  return 0.45 * m + 0.35 * g + 0.2 * e;
}

Picking three is a brute-force loop over every triple. With 59 presets that's about 32,000 triples, which is nothing. A triple is only allowed if all three templates differ or all three animations differ, and if the song has cover art at least one pick has to use it. Triples that differ on both get a small bonus.

What I gave up: the model no longer invents a look nobody has seen before.

What I got: the slow part of the call is gone, every option has been checked by a human eye at least once, and variety now depends on the preset library. Growing that library is my job and doesn't depend on prompt luck.

If the tagging call fails twice, a rules-only fallback picks from the style tags and the song's line density, so the user always gets three options.

v1: LLM designs v2: LLM tags, code picks
LLM returns 3 full Style objects Moods, genres, energy, chorus lines, emphasis words
Who decides the look The model A score over hand-built presets
Where variety comes from Prompt wording Size of the preset library
When the LLM fails Retry, or no video Rules-only fallback

The LLM turned out to be good at the labelling. With section markers stripped out, it called "is this line part of the chorus" correctly on all 178 lines in my test set, twice. Full section labels were 97–98% right. The misses were bridge vs. pre-chorus confusions, which don't change anything visually, because the styling only cares whether a line is in the chorus.

Where the LLM still edits the design

There's one place the model still touches the Style directly: "make the chorus bigger," "warmer colours," "less busy." That request goes to the model along with the current Style, and the model returns an RFC 6902 JSON Patch instead of a new object:

{
  "patch": [
    { "op": "add", "path": "/sections/chorus/typography/scale", "value": 1.35 }
  ],
  "explanation": "Made the chorus lines larger so it lifts."
}

A patch keeps the edit minimal, and the change is easy to show and revert. Every patch is stored as a revision on the project. One gotcha: an add fails if the parent object doesn't exist, and "add /sections/chorus/typography/scale to a chorus with no typography yet" is exactly what the model is told to emit. So before applying the patch I create the missing parent objects. The patched result goes through the same validator, so a "make it moodier" request can't produce unreadable text.

Timing, briefly

The word-by-word timing doesn't use an LLM at all. The audio and the lyric lines go to a forced-alignment API, which returns start and end times plus a per-word loss value. I map those timings back onto our lines by character offset and turn the loss into a 0–1 confidence with a logistic curve (calibrated so a loss of 1.8 maps to 0.6). Lines below 0.6 get flagged in the editor so you can nudge them by hand. Forced alignment is good, but a held note or a backing vocal can still throw it off.

What I'd tell myself at the start

  • If an LLM's output is going to be rendered, write the semantic checks before the prompt. Valid JSON can still be an unreadable frame.
  • "The model designs it" demos better than "the model picks from things a person designed." In daily use the second one is faster and repeats itself less.

If you want to see the result, the free tier of LyricVideoGenerator exports 720p 16:9 without an account.

articles.title: Stop Jamming Translate, Rotate, and Scale Into One `transform`
articles.description: A CSS :hover scale and a JS drag handler both write to `transform` — and the moment JS sets it, the hover rule silently stops working, no error, no warning. The `translate`, `rotate`, and `scale` properties exist so this never happens.
articles.body_html:
You build a product card. On hover, it should lift a little — transform: scale(1.03), a transition, done in five minutes. Then the ticket comes in: cards need to be draggable, so you add a pointermove handler that keeps the card glued to the cursor:

card.style.transform = `translate(${x}px, ${y}px)`;

You test the drag. It works. You test the hover — on a card you haven't dragged yet — and it works too. Then you drag a card, let go, and move your mouse back over it.

Nothing happens. The lift is just gone. No console error, no warning, and the line that broke it isn't even in your CSS file.

The bug nobody writes on purpose

Here's the part that makes this one sneaky: both rules are completely correct on their own.

.card {
  transition: transform 150ms ease;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: scale(1.03);
}

function onDrag(card, x, y) {
  card.style.transform = `translate(${x}px, ${y}px)`;
}

Nobody misspelled a selector. The specificity math even looks like it should favor the pseudo-class most of the time. But specificity isn't what decides this fight — an element's own style attribute beats any selector-based rule for the same property, :hover included, !important aside. The instant onDrag runs once, card.style.transform is set, and from that point forward your stylesheet's .card:hover { transform: scale(1.03) } has nothing left to write to. It still matches. It still "wins" by every specificity rule you learned. The browser just has nowhere to put its answer, because the inline declaration already owns the property.

Open DevTools on a dragged card and look at the Styles panel: you'll see the :hover rule listed, not crossed out, not overridden by anything visible — and still not applied. That's what makes it brutal to debug. Nothing in the inspector tells you an inline style from a completely unrelated JS file is the reason.

The fixes that don't actually fix it

The first instinct is !important:

.card:hover {
  transform: scale(1.03) !important;
}

Now hover wins again — but it wins by replacing the transform outright, not by adding to it. Hover a card mid-drag and it snaps back to wherever scale(1.03) alone would place it, then snaps away again on mouseout. You didn't fix the conflict, you just picked a different single winner for a property that was only ever built to hold one value at a time.

The next instinct is to stop fighting CSS and do it all in JS: track mouseenter/mouseleave, keep the current drag offset and the current hover state in two variables, and rebuild the whole string on every change:

function render() {
  card.style.transform = `translate(${x}px, ${y}px) scale(${hovering ? 1.03 : 1})`;
}

This works. It also means you've reimplemented :hover in JavaScript, with your own event listeners, your own state, and your own transition timing — for a one-line CSS feature the browser already does for free. Add a focus style or a prefers-reduced-motion check and the string-building function keeps growing.

transform was never built to share

The actual problem is one level up: transform is a single property, and a single property can only hold one value. Whoever writes to it last — JS or CSS — wins the whole thing, not just their part of it. There was no way to say "I only care about position, someone else can own the scale" because position and scale lived inside the exact same string.

That stopped being true in 2022. translate, rotate, and scale are now their own CSS properties, independent of transform and independent of each other, supported in every major engine (Chrome and Edge 104+, Firefox 72+, Safari 14.1+) — which by now means every browser your analytics will show you. Give the drag handler one property and the hover rule a different one:

.card {
  scale: 1;
  transition: scale 150ms ease;
}
.card:hover {
  scale: 1.03;
}

function onDrag(card, x, y) {
  card.style.translate = `${x}px ${y}px`;
}

No shared string, no state to track, no !important. JS writes translate every pointermove; the browser handles :hover writing scale the way it always has. Drag a card and its hover lift still fires, because for the first time the two concerns were never fighting for the same property to begin with.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The browser applies these in one fixed order — translate, then rotate, then scale, then whatever's left in transform — no matter what order you declare them in your code. That's worth knowing if you still reach for transform for something the individual properties don't cover, like skew() or a raw matrix(): it always applies last, on top of the other three, not wherever you happened to write it.

Where this hides beyond drag-and-drop

Dragging is the clearest version, but the same collision shows up anywhere JS and CSS both think they own motion on the same element:

  • A parallax or scroll-linked effect that sets transform every frame, on a card that also has a CSS :focus or :active micro-interaction.
  • A FLIP-style animation library that writes a starting transform via JS, racing a stylesheet transition meant to animate it away.
  • A carousel or swiper that positions slides with inline transform, on a component whose design system also wants a CSS-only hover state on each slide.

The symptom is always the same: a CSS rule that's "obviously" correct, matches, shows up in DevTools — and just doesn't apply, because something else got to the property first.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

What this doesn't fix

Individual transform properties don't replace transform — skew(), matrix(), and matrix3d() still only exist inside it, and if two different things both need to animate the same axis (two JS handlers both wanting to own translate, say), you're back to needing one source of truth for that value. What they fix is the specific, common case of position/rotation/scale each belonging to a different piece of code — which covers most of the JS-meets-CSS collisions you'll actually hit.

Next time a hover or focus style "randomly" stops working on an element some other script touches, check whether that script is writing to transform — and if it is, see if giving it translate instead buys your CSS room to breathe again. What's the weirdest "it matches in DevTools but doesn't apply" bug you've chased down? I'd like to hear it.
