articles.title: PHP2Shell: what the two critical PHP RCE CVEs actually mean for your stack
articles.description: If you're on PHP 8.1 or older, there is no official fix coming. Those branches are end-of-life. Your...
articles.body_html:
If you're on PHP 8.1 or older, there is no official fix coming. Those branches are end-of-life. Your options are: upgrade, or ask your hosting/distro vendor if they provide a backported patch (some LTS vendors do).

What to actually do today

1. Check what's really running your site, not just your CLI version

php -v

This shows your CLI version. It is not necessarily the version serving requests. Check the SAPI that's actually live:

php-fpm -v
curl -sI https://yoursite.com/ | grep -iE "^(server|x-powered-by):"

CLI and web versions can differ, especially on servers hosting multiple projects.

2. Patch internet-facing systems first

If it's reachable from the open internet, it's the priority. Internal-only services can wait a few hours if you're triaging a lot of infrastructure.

3. Don't forget bundled PHP

Docker base images, CMS installer bundles, and vendor tarballs often ship their own PHP. A host-level patch won't touch these. Check every running image:

docker exec <container> php -v

4. Ask your hosting provider directly

Managed hosts (SiteGround, Cloudflare-fronted setups, etc.) may have already deployed WAF-level mitigations or patched server-side. Don't assume — ask.

5. Watch for post-exploitation signs

Keep an eye on PHP worker processes spawning shells, curl/wget calls, or unexpected outbound connections. That's the pattern seen in active exploitation so far.

A stopgap, not a fix

Some researchers have floated disabling session.upload_progress as a temporary mitigation:

session.upload_progress.enabled = Off

This is not a substitute for patching. Treat it as something you do while you're rolling out the real fix, not instead of it.

If you manage sites for other people

Send a short, plain update today — what happened, what you're doing about it, when it'll be done. Clients hearing about a "PHP vulnerability" from the news before they hear it from you is a worse conversation than this one.

Sources:

  • PHP.net security archive
  • watchTowr PHP2Shell FAQ
  • Help Net Security writeup
  • Wiz Research disclosure

Has your stack been patched yet? Drop your setup in the comments — curious how many people are finding PHP buried in places they forgot about.

articles.title: One Game Engine, Three Word Games: How I Built the Krillion Family
articles.description: Most word games reward the obvious answer. I wanted the opposite.  Krillion gives everyone the same...
articles.body_html:
Most word games reward the obvious answer. I wanted the opposite.

Krillion gives everyone the same prompt — "Name a fruit" — and scores you on how rare your answers are. Say what everyone says and you stay near the surface. Find the answer nobody else thinks of and you dive deep. Your score is literally a depth.

That one idea turned into three live games, all running on a single engine:

  • 🎯 Dive Krillion — the daily game. One dive a day, plus Unlimited, Marathon and Challenge modes, 8 category packs, and a guest leaderboard.
  • ♾️ Krillion Infinite — the endless version. No daily limit, just keep diving.
  • 🔁 Noillirk — the backwards game. Same DNA, but you have to think in reverse. (Yes, the name is "Krillion" backwards.)

The stack

  • Next.js on Vercel for all three sites
  • Supabase — auth, cloud-saved dive records, and the guest leaderboard (Postgres)
  • A shared game engine: a 302-prompt bank, a rarity-scoring model with tiers (common answers score shallow, deep cuts score big), and depth-meter game feel — answers sink, the water darkens as you go deeper
  • PWA + web push — a daily reminder when the new dive drops
  • Satori-generated share cards — every finished dive becomes a 1200×700 PNG score card players can share

Three sites, one codebase philosophy

I didn't build three games. I built one engine and three rule sets:

  • Dive Krillion = the daily ritual. One shared dive per day, records in the cloud, streaks and history matter.
  • Krillion Infinite = the same engine with the daily lock removed and the content reorganised around endless play.
  • Noillirk = the engine mirrored. Prompts and answers run backwards, which sounds like a joke until you play it — your brain genuinely has to rewire.

Theming, rules and content differ; the core (prompts, scoring, tiers, audio, share cards) is shared. Shipping a fix once ships it everywhere.

Lessons that cost me real hours

1. "Midnight" is not a timezone.
Dive Krillion resets at midnight Eastern. Krillion Infinite resets at midnight your local time. Two lines of product copy, two completely different implementations — and players notice immediately when a reset feels wrong. Decide your reset semantics early and write them on the site, in the FAQ, where players can see them.

2. Performance is a feature, not a cleanup task.
These are games people open for 90 seconds on their phones. I got the twin sites to 90–97 on mobile PageSpeed, and the wins were mostly removals: reserving exact layout space from first paint so nothing shifts, deferring engine setup until after first render, lazy-loading analytics, and deleting a decorative poster image that cost more LCP than it was worth. What I removed mattered more than what I added.

3. The share card is the growth loop.
Players don't share links; they share scores. The moment a finished dive produced a good-looking PNG card — depth, stats, "CAN YOU GO DEEPER?" — sharing stopped being a feature I built and became something players just do. If you build a daily game, budget real design time for the card.

4. Accounts should be invisible until they're useful.
Guests can play and appear on the leaderboard without signing up. Accounts exist for one reason: your records follow you across phone and laptop. Conversion into signups took care of itself once the account had an obvious job.

Try them

  • Daily dive: divekrillion.com
  • Endless mode: krillioninfinite.com
  • Backwards mode: krillioninfinite.online

All three are free, no download, works on any phone browser.

I'd genuinely love feedback from other builders: how would you handle the daily-reset problem across timezones? And if you play a dive — how deep did you get?

articles.title: Don't Be a Proxy Between Me and Your AI
articles.description: I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.  I raise a technical question in a...
articles.body_html:
I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.

I raise a technical question in a thread, a meeting, or a design review and someone responds with a long, well-structured, suspiciously balanced answer. It has headers in spirit if not in format, it covers 3 tradeoffs and ends with a neat recommendation.

I push back on one point. Silence for a minute, the kind where you can practically hear a browser tab switching. Then another equally polished paragraph appears, answering my pushback.

At some point it kinda gives: I'm not talking to a colleague. I'm talking to a chat window with a human-shaped copy-paste button attached.

please stop doing that, I'm practically begging you.

I Can Open a Browser Too

Let me say the obvious thing first. If I wanted to debate an AI, I'd debate an AI. I can type a question into ChatGPT, Claude, or whatever else is in vogue this week. It takes me 10 seconds, and I'd get to skip the middleman. Right now you're less a colleague and more a loading spinner with a LinkedIn profile.

When I bring a technical question to you, I’m asking for your judgment. What you’ve seen work, what you’ve watched fail, and what taught you the difference. I want to know which tradeoffs you’d accept, which assumptions you’d challenge, and why. That’s the experience I’m interested in hearing.

The moment you become a pass-through, I lose all of that. I'm getting generic output with your name on it, and you've added latency to the conversation without adding anything else. Congratulations, you've invented the world's slowest API wrapper.

"But I'm the Decision-Maker"

This is the one that really gets me.

The pitch goes like this: in the AI era, the developer's job is to be the "architect". The AI generates the options, the human decides. You're like the guardrail, the one with taste.

Fine model. I think it's genuinely where a lot of the job is heading.

But a decision-maker who agrees with the AI's recommendation 99% of the time isn't deciding anything. That's a rubber stamp with a job title. If your "decisions" are indistinguishable from the model's default output, then you haven't added a layer of judgment, you've just added a layer of delay.

So here's a simple test: can you name a recent time you disagreed with the AI, and why? Not "I tweaked the formatting." A real disagreement, grounded in something the model couldn't know, like a constraint, a past incident, or a team preference.

If you can't, you're not the guardrail. You're the passenger and you didn't even pick the playlist.

I have a good, real example of this:

Someone messaged me on LinkedIn, saying they were interested in learning how I approach problems in distributed systems. I'll be honest: that's the kind of message that makes my day. A person wants to talk shop, and wants my thinking.

So I engaged. I walked through how I reason about failure modes and where I start when things go inconsistent and we went back and forth for a while.

Then I found out they'd been using an AI to debate me the whole time. They hadn't come to learn from me at all. They'd come to argue with me through a proxy.

And here's the thing: I debate AI every day. By choice, on my own terms, whenever I feel like it. That part is easy to get. What's rare is another human being who's actually willing to sit in the conversation, think out loud, be wrong in front of me, and push back with their own head.

If they'd just asked me their own half-formed questions, I'd have answered them all day.

"Whatever the AI Said Is What I Agree With"

This is the response I get when I ask the follow-up: "What's the point of discussing this if your brain isn't the one engaging?"

"Oh, well, it's what I agree with anyway."

Bold of you to agree so passionately with a position you didn't form.

Agreement without understanding is not the same as agreement. If I ask why you agree and the honest answer is "because it said so and it sounded right," then you don't hold a position but a borrowed one.

And borrowed positions collapse under the first real question, like a Jenga tower in a minor earthquake. I wrote about this before: reading something and nodding is not the same skill as being able to produce or defend it. A discussion is exactly the situation that exposes the gap, which is why it matters.

And about the "I'm verifying the output" defense: verification is real work. It means checking claims against reality, testing assumptions, and spotting what's subtly wrong. If your verification consists of reading the answer and thinking "yep, sounds right," that's not a guardrail, that's reading. A guardrail that never catches anything is just a decorative pool noodle.

"I Don't Have Time, I'm Busy"

classic. "I just don't have time to dig into this, so I asked the AI."

Yah yah, you're busy but so is everyone. I am busy. The person you're talking to is busy. The barista making your oat flat white is busy. Busy is not a personality. Being busy isn't a special condition you hold exclusively and it doesn't excuse you from engaging with the thing you chose to join a discussion about.

But notice the quiet logic buried in that excuse: if you don't have time to engage, you also don't have time to be in the conversation. There's a clean, honorable option here, and it's just saying so:

"I don't have the bandwidth to think this through properly. I'd rather not give you a half-answer. Can we circle back later today?"

It's respectable, It's honest, it respects my time and it doesn't pretend. What's not respectable is dumping unvetted output into the thread and presenting it as your contribution.

The Fair Counterargument

Before this turns into pure ranting, let me steelman the other side and because there are legitimate reasons someone leans on AI in discussions:

  • Language. If English isn’t your first language, using AI to polish your phrasing is a perfectly good use. What matters is that the ideas are yours. And honestly, I don’t care if your spelling or grammar is rough. I’m a software engineer, not an English literature professor. The point of language is to communicate ideas. If I understand what you’re trying to say—and 99% of the time, I do—we’re good.
  • Preparation. Using AI to explore a topic beforehand, surface counterarguments, or sanity-check your thinking is great. That's research.
  • Juniors learning. Someone new may reach for AI because they don't yet have the experience to form an opinion. That's understandable, and the fix is mentoring, not shaming.

I don't have a problem with AI being in the process. I have a problem with AI replacing the person in the process.

The line, I think, is this: did you take the model's output and make it yours? Did you push on it, disagree with parts of it, and rewrite it in terms of your actual situation? Or did you relay it?

Try these

Here's how I think AI belongs in a technical discussion:

  1. Use it before the conversation, not during it. Ask it to stress-test your idea. Ask it for the strongest objection. Then think about the answer.
  2. Form a position you can defend without it. If someone challenges you and you'd need to go back to the chat window to answer, you're not ready to answer.
  3. Be upfront about what's yours and what isn't. "I asked an AI for options and I'm leaning toward B because of X" is excellent. The "because of X" is the part that proves a human was involved.
  4. Disagree with it sometimes, on purpose. If you never override the model, ask yourself whether you're evaluating it or just following it.
  5. When you don't know, say so. "I don't know, let me find out" has never made anyone look incompetent. Faking it with someone else's words eventually does.

Why This Matters Beyond Politeness

It's tempting to file all of this under "annoying etiquette," but I think it's bigger than that.

Technical discussion is how teams build a shared mental model. It's where assumptions get surfaced, where one person's experience corrects another's blind spot, and where the real reasoning behind decisions gets created and recorded. If one side of the conversation is hollow, the team walks away with a decision that nobody actually reasoned about.

That's the same cognitive-debt problem I keep writing about, just moved from code into conversation. And like all debt, it comes due at a bad moment, usually when the decision turns out to be wrong and someone asks, "Why did we choose this?" and the honest answer is "the AI said so, and we all kind of nodded."

Conclusion

Use AI. Use it constantly, if it makes you better. But when you sit down to talk to another human about a hard problem, show up.

Bring your own opinions, even imperfect ones, bring your own doubts, bring the thing you know that the model doesn't. That's the only thing I came to the conversation for.

Because if I wanted the average of the internet's opinion, I'd have asked the internet. Human engagement is the rare thing now so please don't be the reason it gets rarer.

articles.title: Nothing Reported It
articles.description: Five ways my own test harness lied to me, and the one that nearly got published   The number...
articles.body_html:
Five ways my own test harness lied to me, and the one that nearly got published

The number that gave it away was sitting in a table I had already read three times.

prompt size    97 tokens median, 112 max

That is the grounded question-answering workflow. It sends four reference documents with every question. The documents are 447 words.

Four hundred and forty-seven words cannot be ninety-seven tokens.

I had written that number into a results document as good news about context headroom. "Prompt sizes never approached the 4096-token context window." It was not good news about headroom. It was the harness telling me, in the only field capable of telling me, that the reference material was not in the prompt. The directory holding it had never been committed to the repository. Every one of those fifteen questions had been asked against an empty reference block.

Both models had behaved impeccably. One had been instructed to answer NOT IN THE MATERIAL when the material did not contain the answer, and the material contained nothing, so it said NOT IN THE MATERIAL thirteen times out of fifteen. The other had no such instruction, so it answered from whatever it had memorized during training and invented a wine.

Every call returned 200. The scorer scored it. The scores were internally consistent, had plausible and different failure modes on each side, and I wrote two thousand seven hundred words about what they revealed regarding the capabilities of small language models.

They revealed nothing about small language models. I had measured what happens when you ask a question with no reference material, which is a question I was not asking and which has an uninteresting answer.

This is the post about that, and about the four other things I found in the same weekend, because the missing directory was not the first one and it was not even the most instructive.

The experiment, briefly

A Raspberry Pi 4, two small models through Ollama, and three workflows: pull an identifier out of a message, route a message to one of six queues, answer a question from four documents. Ninety-five test cases. A deterministic baseline for the first workflow. Predictions committed before anything was installed.

The findings are a separate post. This one is about the code I wrote to produce them, which turned out to be where the actual bugs were.

Five flaws. Every single one was found by reading output, not by reading code. I never once found one of these by looking at the scorer.

Kind one: a metric that rewards the safe failure

This one I hit twice, in two different workflows, and did not recognize the second instance as the same bug until I had already fixed the first.

The classification scorer. Six labels, one of which is escalate. The instruction said to escalate when a message needs a person, including when you cannot tell what it is about. So I built a metric called confident wrong: wrong, and not an escalation. The reasoning is sound. A model that escalates when unsure is usable. A model that routes a trademark notice to billing is not.

Then the 360M model answered escalate to 43 of 50 messages.

It scored 3 on confident wrong. The 1.5B model, which was genuinely attempting the task and getting 46% of it right, scored 26.

My metric had just certified the useless model as roughly six times safer than the mediocre one. Because escalations are exempt, a model that escalates always cannot register a confident error. The exemption I added to reward caution had instead rewarded paralysis, and it did so in the direction that looks best.

The grounded QA scorer. Four of the fifteen questions have no answer in the corpus. Correctly saying so is the behavior that matters most, because a system that invents a plausible answer with no evidence is worse than one that fails loudly: it is indistinguishable from one that worked. So the headline number was correct abstentions out of four.

Then the 1.5B model said NOT IN THE MATERIAL to 13 of 15 questions.

It scored 4 out of 4. A perfect score, on the metric I cared most about, for a model that had answered almost nothing.

Same bug. Different workflow. Two hours apart. I fixed the classification one, wrote a comment in the code explaining the principle, and then failed to apply that principle to the file I opened next.

The shape, stated once: a metric that rewards the safe behavior will certify any model that only ever does the safe thing. If you exempt a behavior because it is cautious, you have to pair that exemption with evidence that the model is making distinctions at all. Otherwise, the exemption is the score.

Both fixes are the same three lines: count how concentrated the answers are, and when one answer dominates, print a warning that the headline number is meaningless and say why.

Kind two: a metric that measures nothing at all

The vacuous fixture. I caught this one before the run, which is the only reason it is not a bigger part of this post. A test case that passed regardless of what the model did, because the fixture was inert either way. It contributed a tick to a column and no information.

The keyword check, which is worse, because it survived longer and looked more useful.

The eleven answerable QA questions each carry a list of words the correct answer should contain. The scorer checks whether any of them appear anywhere in the reply. I labeled it "indicative only" and moved on.

On the invalid run it scored 1 of 11 for both models. The single hit was the word "reservation", appearing inside this answer:

You owe a tasting fee of $100 for the weekend. You also need to book a reservation for the weekend.

The correct fee is forty dollars. The hundred is invented. That one hit was the entire positive signal in my automated QA scoring and it was noise.

Here is the part that makes it a better story. After I fixed the corpus and reran, the keyword check scored 11 of 11 for the 1.5B model. Vindicated, apparently. I read all eleven answers by hand anyway, and nine of them are right.

So the check was wrong both times. It was wrong in the pessimistic direction when the answers were bad and wrong in the optimistic direction when they were good, and on the rerun one of its eleven hits is an answer that gets the arithmetic wrong and hits on the word "reservation" anyway.

A check that agrees with the truth because the truth happened to be agreeable has not been validated. It has been lucky.

Kind three: a detector with a blind spot in the obvious direction

I wrote a decay check because of a thermal problem. A Pi 4 with heat sinks and no fan hit its soft temperature limit during a thirty-call run and started capping the clock, and nothing anywhere said so. So the scorer now compares generation speed in the first third of a run to the last third and flags a slowdown.

It then reported this, as steady:

across the run 4.3 -> 7.6 tok/s (176% of starting speed, steady)

The hardware got seventy-six percent faster partway through a run. My detector, which was looking for numbers below a threshold, saw a number above it and reported no problem.

Hardware does not speed up. That reading is either contention at the start of the run or, as it turned out, generations too short to time. Either way it is a signal that the measurement is unreliable, and I had built a detector that would only ever notice half of the ways that can happen.

Anything you threshold in one direction, threshold in both. An implausibly good number is as informative as an implausibly bad one and nobody ever writes the check for it.

Kind four: errors that get dropped instead of counted

Partway through the first extraction run, Ollama returned a 500 and the runner died at case seven of thirty. The traceback was useless because urllib raises HTTPError and discards the response body, which is where Ollama puts its reason. Reading e.read() gave it up immediately:

{"error":"prediction aborted, token repeat limit reached"}

The 360M model, asked to find an order number in "Thanks for a lovely afternoon yesterday," where the correct answer is one word, had fallen into a repetition loop and been killed after twenty-one seconds. Reproducible at temperature zero. The input causes it.

My first fix was to record failures and keep going, which was right. My second was to exclude all failures from the scores as infrastructure noise, which was badly wrong.

That call was not infrastructure noise. The model ran. It received the prompt, generated tokens, and produced nothing usable. That is a result, and excluding it would have dropped from the denominator the single case this model demonstrably could not handle, scoring it only on the cases it survived.

So the runner now tags every failure as one of two kinds:

  • Model failure. The call reached a working model and the model failed. Stays in the denominator. Counts against the model. Reported on its own line as "no usable answer."
  • Transport failure. The call never reached a working model. Ollama was down, the tag was wrong, the request timed out. Nothing was measured, so it is excluded and the run is reported as incomplete.

The distinction is a five-line change and it is the difference between measuring a model and measuring a model on the subset of inputs it happens to tolerate.

Kind five: inputs that go missing without raising

This is the missing corpus from the top of the post, and it is a different and worse category than everything above it.

The function was four lines:

def corpus_text():
    parts = []
    for p in sorted((FIX / "corpus").glob("*.md")):
        parts.append(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())
    return "\n\n".join(parts)

A glob that matches nothing yields nothing. An empty list joins to the empty string. No exception, no warning, no exit code. It returns a perfectly valid value that happens to be the absence of the thing it was asked for.

And on the same evening, a sibling. The offline test's entire product is a text transcript. I copied it into the run directory, committed, pushed, and it was not there. The standard Python .gitignore template, which I had pulled in wholesale, carries *.log on line 165, and a pattern without a leading slash matches at any depth.

The copy succeeded. git status came back clean. The push reported success. The one artifact the test exists to produce was gone, and everything in the chain said fine.

Absence does not raise. A missing directory, a missing file and an inert fixture all present as an ordinary successful run. That is narrower and more useful than "test your tests," and it generalizes: every input a harness depends on needs a loader that refuses to proceed without it, and every artifact it produces needs to be verified as present rather than inferred from an exit status.

The loader now looks like this, and the comment is longer than the code because the comment is the part I will need next year:

paths = sorted(corpus_dir.glob("*.md"))
if not paths:
    raise SystemExit(
        f"No corpus documents found in {corpus_dir}\n"
        "Grounded QA cannot run without reference material, and running\n"
        "it against an empty reference block produces numbers that look\n"
        "like a result."
    )

It also refuses a corpus implausibly smaller than the real one, the run prints the document count and token estimate before its first call, and the scorer independently flags any QA run whose median prompt is under 400 tokens. Three checks for one bug, in the input, in the run, and in the output, because this is the bug that cost a day.

The detector that fired, and was right, and told me the wrong thing

Here is the part I find hardest to write and most worth keeping.

The abstention-collapse check from kind one did fire on the invalid run. It printed exactly this:

!! ABSTAINED on 13/15 questions overall. It is refusing, not judging.
   The abstention score below is not evidence of discrimination:
   a model that never answers gets it right for free.

It was correct. Something was badly wrong with that run.

Its diagnosis was completely false. The model was not refusing. It was obeying, precisely, an instruction to report when the material lacks the answer, in a situation where the material lacked everything. The fault was not in the model's judgment, and it was not in the metric. It was in a directory that did not exist, two layers upstream.

And I acted on the diagnosis. I wrote it up: the model has a stuck needle, its perfect abstention score is an artifact of refusal, here are the implications for anyone building on a 1.5B model. Confident, specific, sourced to real output, and wrong in every particular.

A flag that tells you something is off is not a flag that tells you what. The check could only see the output. The fault was in the input. It fired for the right reason and pointed in the wrong direction, and because it fired I felt more confident in a conclusion that was false, not less.

That is the failure mode I had no defense against and still only partly do. A monitoring system that is right about the existence of a problem and wrong about its cause is more dangerous than no monitoring, because it terminates the search.

What I actually changed

For anyone who wants the diffs rather than the moral:

  • Collapse checks on both classification and QA: when one answer exceeds half the set, print the concentration and declare the headline metric meaningless for that model.
  • The decay check flags implausible speedups as well as slowdowns, and notes when generations are too short to time.
  • Failures split into model and transport, with model failures staying in the denominator.
  • corpus_text() raises on an empty or implausibly small corpus.
  • The QA run prints its corpus size before the first call.
  • The scorer flags a QA run whose prompts are too small to contain the corpus.
  • The keyword check is relabelled as a weak lower bound, in the output, in the README, and in the results.
  • .gitignore no longer lets *.log swallow run transcripts.
  • vcgencmd get_throttled before and after every run, recorded in the run document rather than checked and forgotten. The reading reports bits set since boot, so it is perishable: power-cycle the board and the evidence is gone.

The uncomfortable part

Every one of these was found by looking at data. Not one was found by reading code, reviewing the scorer, or writing a unit test for the harness.

The vacuous fixture turned up while hand-checking a passing case. The confident-wrong flaw turned up because a score of 3 against 26 looked backwards. The abstention flaw turned up because 4 out of 4 looked too good. The keyword flaw turned up because 1 of 11 looked too bad, and I read the one. The missing corpus turned up because I was double-checking a latency figure and noticed a prompt that was too small to be possible.

Which means the only reason I found them is that I kept pulling threads after I had numbers that looked publishable. The version of this project that shipped on schedule shipped on Tuesday, with a clean verdict table, a confident conclusion about small models and grounded question answering, and a repository anyone could clone to reproduce the exact same wrong result.

Every number in it would have been reproducible. That is the thing I keep turning over. Reproducibility is table stakes and it would not have saved me, because the harness reproduced its own bug faithfully every single time.

I do not have a process that catches this reliably. What I have is a weaker and more honest claim: the checks I added are each a direct response to one specific thing that actually happened, which is the only kind of check I trust, and the number of them that I thought up in advance is zero.

So the two rows I am adding to my prediction template, to be filled in before anything runs:

  • What would have to be true for these numbers to be meaningless?
  • Would anything in the harness tell me if it were?

Twenty-two predictions about what the models would do. Not one about what the measuring code would do. Four of the five flaws were in the measuring code.

The harness, the fixtures, the committed predictions and the full run record, including the invalid run and what it produced, are at
github.com/kenwalger/right-size-the-model.
The findings the harness eventually produced are in the companion post.

articles.title: 926 Steps, Two Lobotomies, and Zero Nudges: Flight-Testing the Commitment Machine Across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS
articles.description: A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI agents write 30% more code and close zero additional tickets because review times jump 49%. Here is what happened when I put my 1986 Commitment Machine into live production across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS.
articles.body_html:
A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI coding agents write 30% more code and close zero extra tickets because PR review times jump 49%. When I ran my 1986 Commitment Machine across five live production tickets, a mid-flight vendor swap, and an open-weight crash test, here is what the flight recorder proved.

"The dashboard with the Mermaid state diagram is perfect. I find myself not even opening the pull requests now. I just wait for the green board or the triage details... And I also like that every code change is paired with an immediate critical reviewer. That one step really reduces friction."

— My notes to myself after the fourth ticket in a row

1. The Bottom Line Up Front: What Live Production Just Proved

Earlier this month, Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton published a massive study ("Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production", covered in Forkast News) tracking 718 companies and more than 725,000 software developers from 2021 to 2026.

By early 2026, over 95% of those companies had rolled out AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin). And the numbers they found should make every engineering manager wince:

  • Developers wrote +30% more code (1,500 extra lines per developer per month), and opened +23% more pull requests.
  • Yet the number of finished Jira tickets and epics went up by 0%.
  • Why? Because PR review wait times jumped +49% (+3.45 days), the number of PRs kicked back for rewrites nearly doubled, review comments per PR rose +35%, and 14% more senior engineers got dragged away from their own work to pay what the researchers call the "babysitting tax."

If you've ever worked on a real software team, you don't need an economics degree to spot the bug. If you make typing code 10x faster, but your AI never pushes back on a bad ticket and never catches its own bugs before committing, you haven't sped up your team. You've just aimed a firehose of plausible-looking slop at your senior reviewers.

In Part 3.10, I redesigned my coding workflow (Randal's Public Workflow Gist) specifically to invert that bottleneck—moving ticket pushback, adversarial code review, and state tracking before git commit using Fernando Flores's 1986 "Committed Speech" rules, a 1976 Makefile, and a 1983 /etc/init.d state directory (00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md).

Then I turned the key and ran five consecutive production tickets (926+ steps, 18 subagents), a 960-step mid-flight vendor swap, and a 791-step open-weight torture test through it.

Before we look at the flight logs, here is the bottom line from those runs:

  1. You beat the +30% code-bloat trap before writing a single line of code: When you force a read-only Codebase Archaeologist subagent to check a ticket's claims against git log before the agent is allowed to promise code, stale or already-solved tickets get closed in 8 minutes via a Counter-Offer (0 lines of code written) or trimmed in half—instead of turning into 300-line zombie PRs.
  2. You beat the +49% PR review bottleneck by running an Adversarial Critic before git commit and collapsing bot threads into one table: Pairing every code edit with a local Critic subagent and a single consolidated PR triage comment catches subtle framework bugs (like Flutter's post-await ScaffoldMessenger trap) locally, so the human reviewer doesn't even have to open the GitHub PR page until the board is green.
  3. Keeping state in /etc/init.d files on disk makes your agent both lobotomy-proof and vendor-agnostic: When every commitment lives in numbered Markdown files on disk instead of hidden inside one model's chat RAM, the agent not only survives back-to-back 200k-token context resets without losing its place—you can literally swap Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 at Step 433 of a 960-step run when a quota wall hits, and the new model finishes the job without missing a beat.
  4. External Makefile scaffolding has a hard floor—and a 120B open-weight model fell right through it: A Makefile can keep a capable model (Gemini 4 or Claude Sonnet 4.6) on the rails, but when I put GPT-OSS 120B into the exact same cockpit for 791 steps, it ignored the /etc/init.d files, suffered 6 context lobotomies, searched Google for private local Dart classes, and fork-bombed 6 simultaneous background git commit jobs while deleting .git/index.lock.

2. Why These Five Tickets Matter: Every One of Them Tests a Different Failure Mode

I didn't cherry-pick five easy toy problems. These were simply the next five tickets sitting in our production monorepo backlog—and each one happened to test a specific failure mode where normal AI coding agents create work instead of finishing it:

Ticket & The Failure Mode It Tested Steps / Subagents Context Resets What the Commitment Machine Did Differently Dev Nudges
1. TICKET-553: The Stale / Contradicted Ticket
(Tests whether the agent blindly writes +30% dead code on an obsolete ticket) 		69 steps
1 subagent		 0 Archaeologist proved the requested wrapper was already built and rejected in PR #927 two weeks ago. Issued a Counter-Offer: closed in 8m 29s with 0 lines of code. 0
2. TICKET-779: The Half-Solved Ticket
(Tests whether the agent re-implements work that already landed on main) 		135 steps
3 subagents		 0 Archaeologist proved the .scripts/*.sh pipefail guards had already landed in PR #1029, cutting the scope in half (AGENTS.md 31,248 / 32,000 byte cap only). 0
3. TICKET-482: The Linter Blind Spot & Bot Flood
(Tests whether subtle UI bugs and 14 bot threads get dumped on a human reviewer) 		189 steps
5 subagents		 2 Scoped 19 dialogs down to 15, caught a post-await ScaffoldMessenger bug (SCAR-RIV-14) that flutter analyze missed, and triaged 14 bot comments in 1 table. 0
4. TICKET-891: The Flaky Cloud CI Runner
(Tests whether a transient GitHub Actions hiccup drags a human back to babysit) 		182 steps
4 subagents		 0 Verified all 6 ticket premises in 38s, passed 2 Critic rounds, and automatically re-ran a flaky cloud CI job (gh run rerun --failed) to green. 0
5. TICKET-227: The Double Context Lobotomy
(Tests whether a 351-step math/binary ticket falls apart when the 200k window resets mid-commit) 		351 steps
5 subagents		 2 (233k & 46k) Hit auto-compaction 1 second after I said "ok to commit and push". Woke up, read 00_governance.md..99_next_action.md, and finished 45/45 tests with 0 reminders. 0

Let's walk through how these five tickets, the mid-flight Claude-to-Gemini swap, and the GPT-OSS 120B crash test played out in the transcripts.

3. Finding #1: Beating the +30% Code-Bloat Trap Before Writing a Single Line of Code (TICKET-553, TICKET-779, TICKET-482)

Why did the 718 companies in the Harvard study end up with +30% more code and 0% more finished tickets?

Because in a real engineering backlog, tickets rot. Between the day somebody files a ticket and the day an engineer picks it up, other PRs merge, architecture decisions change, and half the work often gets solved somewhere else.

Hand a normal AI agent a stale ticket, and its "Yes-Man" training (Part 3.9) forces it to say "Certainly!" and write the code anyway:

  • On TICKET-779, the ticket asked to add set -euo pipefail guards to our .scripts/*.sh files and enforce a 32 KB size limit on AGENTS.md. Before writing a plan, my Target 15 Archaeologist checked the repo, proved the .sh scripts already had set -euo pipefail on main, and cut the job in half.
  • On TICKET-482, the ticket listed 19 creation dialogs that needed error-banner handling. The Archaeologist inspected all 19 up front, proved 4 of them were already fixed on main, and scoped the plan strictly to the remaining 15.

And then there was TICKET-553—the poster child for the Harvard study's +30% code bloat.

TICKET-553 was a High priority ticket asking the developer to build a pre-signout wrapper (PreSignOutFirebaseAuth) that deletes the user's push-notification token from the database before calling FirebaseAuth.instance.signOut().

If you only look at today's files on HEAD, that wrapper isn't there—so a standard AI agent would happily crank out ~280 lines of code across 4 files and open a pull request.

Instead, my Target 15 Codebase Archaeologist ran git log -p across recent history (SCAR-ARCH-20) and wrote down a devastating finding in 15_archaeology_receipt.md:

  • Two weeks after TICKET-553 was filed, a developer working on a sibling ticket in PR #927 had already written that exact 243-line PreSignOutFirebaseAuth wrapper!
  • During code review on PR #927, our human lead architect explicitly rejected the wrapper, explaining that wrapping FirebaseAuth is brittle across SDK upgrades and unnecessary because post-signout cleanup + server-side pruning already handles stale tokens. A follow-up commit deleted the wrapper before PR #927 merged—leaving the older duplicate TICKET-553 sitting forgotten in the backlog like an unexploded bomb!

Because our workflow stamps any ticket claim that collides with codebase history as CONTRADICTED, the agent was forbidden to promise code. Instead, it came back to me with a Counter-Offer:

  • Plan A (Recommended — 0 files, 0 lines of code): Accept the Archaeologist's receipt, skip coding, post the PR #927 history onto TICKET-553, and close the ticket.
  • Plan B (4 files, ~280 lines of code): Overrule the lead architect and build the rejected wrapper anyway.

My entire review took four seconds: "plan A is fine. If he has already spoken, I'm not challenging."

Even better, because our workflow is a 1976 Makefile rather than a rigid 21-step checklist, an approved plan with zero target files didn't require any GOTO spaghetti: Target 30 (code), Target 40 (critic), Target 50 (commit), Target 60 (push), and Target 70 (PR checks) all reported Up to date (Nothing to be done) automatically, jumping straight to Target 80 to document and close the issue in 8 minutes, 29 seconds.

4. Finding #2: Beating the +49% Review Bottleneck with Pre-Commit Critics and One-Shot Bot Triage (TICKET-482)

What happens when a ticket does require changing 15 files across four packages?

In the Harvard study, developers push the AI's first green test straight to GitHub, where human reviewers wait 3.45 days only to bounce the PR back (2x bounce rate) or drown in +35% more bot comments.

In TICKET-482 (PR #1234), we saw how the Commitment Machine stops both problems before a human ever opens the PR:

A. Catching a Sneaky Flutter Linter Blind Spot (SCAR-RIV-14)

While updating the 15 creation dialogs so failed saves keep the modal open and display an error banner, the agent wrote the textbook Flutter pattern to satisfy the use_build_context_synchronously lint—capturing ScaffoldMessenger.of(context) and AppLocalizations.of(context) before the await line:

// Captured before the await so use_build_context_synchronously is happy:
final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context);
final local = AppLocalizations.of(context);

final result = await notifier.create(...);
isLoading.value = false;

// ⚠️ THE LINTER BLIND SPOT (SCAR-RIV-14):
notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local);
if (!result.hasError && result.hasValue && context.mounted) {
  Navigator.of(context).pop(result.value);
}

Because the word context doesn't appear inside notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local), flutter analyze --fatal-infos passed with 0 warnings!

Yet if the user closes the modal while await notifier.create(...) is waiting on the network, messenger (which belongs to the parent screen behind the dialog) is still alive—so notifier.onCreated(...) pops up a ghost SnackBar on the parent screen after the modal is already gone!

Instead of a senior engineer having to catch that subtle bug on GitHub three days later:

  1. Our automated review triage (Target 70) flagged the unguarded post-await call.
  2. The TDD Implementation Engineer wrote a Completer<void> widget test that closed the dialog mid-flight and proved the ghost SnackBar bug failed (red_exit = 1).
  3. It wrapped notifier.onCreated, any post-await ref.read(...), and Navigator.pop inside a single outer if (context.mounted) { ... } block (green_exit = 0), and a fresh Round 2 Model: "pro" Adversarial Critic (40_critic_review.md) verified all 14 dialogs before asking me to land.
  4. At Target 90, that trap was permanently recorded as SCAR-RIV-14 so no future agent gets fooled by pre-await ScaffoldMessenger handles.

B. One-Comment Bot Triage & The Mermaid Cockpit (SCAR-PROC-127)

When the GitHub review bot flagged that context.mounted pattern across 14 dialog files (C-1..C-14), our old rules would have burned 28 separate API calls (14 REST +1 reactions + 14 GraphQL resolveReviewThread calls) just closing threads one by one.

At Step 330, I made a simple observation: "generally, we just post one final PR comment instead of closing threads... Yeah, per-thread resolution burns a lot of redundant tokens." That became SCAR-PROC-127: the agent posts one consolidated PR triage table (gh pr comment <PR> --body-file <scratch>/triage_comment.md), paired with our 2-Push Bot Circuit Breaker (SCAR-REVIEW-27) so the agent never gets stuck in an endless ping-pong loop over minor Round 2 bot nitpicks.

And because 99_next_action.md renders a live color-coded Mermaid Commitment Diagram (:::done green, :::active blue, :::gate gold) right in my IDE sidebar, I don't even open the GitHub PR page anymore—I just wait for the green board.

5. Finding #3: /etc/init.d Files Make Your Agent Both Lobotomy-Proof (TICKET-227) and Vendor-Agnostic (Claude -> Gemini at Step 433)

The third reason long AI coding sessions fail in production is that the model either runs out of context tokens (200k lobotomy) or runs out of provider quota halfway through a big ticket.

Because our workflow keeps all commitment state in numbered Unix files on disk (<brain>/state/00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md) and forces subagents (fork()) to do the heavy reading and testing in their own throwaway windows (SCAR-PROC-95), we survived two extreme stress tests:

  1. Surviving Two Context Resets (TICKET-227): On TICKET-227 (351 steps, 45 unit tests), the IDE hit its context limit and triggered auto-compaction (CHECKPOINT) at Step 188 (233,658 -> 43,077 tokens)—literally 1 second after I typed "ok to commit and push"—and then hit a second reset at Step 350. In a normal chat session, getting lobotomized right after "ok to commit and push" is fatal: the model forgets whether the Critic ran or what it was about to commit. With Target 00: read-init-d, the agent woke up on Step 189, read 00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md off the disk, and picked up on the very next tool call with 0 nudges.
  2. Swapping Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 in Mid-Air (Step 433 of 960): During a marathon 960-step UI verification run on PR #1234 (FT-184, booting local emulators and driving an iOS Simulator to capture 5 live screenshots), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Thinking) hit its provider quota wall and died at Step 432. Instead of starting over, I clicked the IDE model picker, switched from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Gemini 4, and typed "continue". At Step 434, Gemini 4 read the /etc/init.d files Claude had written to disk, saw the exact target state, fixed the Xcode 26 simulator window issue in 20 steps, captured all 5 iOS screenshots, and finished the run!

When your workflow state lives in plain text files on disk instead of inside one vendor's context window, the LLM is just a swappable CPU running against a persistent hard drive.

6. Finding #4: The Capability Floor—Why GPT-OSS 120B Crashed and Burned in the Same Cockpit (791 Steps)

That mid-flight swap from Claude to Gemini begged the obvious question:

If the smarts live in the external Makefile and /etc/init.d files on disk, how small or cheap a model can wear the suit? Can you drop an open-weight 120B model into the exact same cockpit and get a senior engineer for free?

To find out, I took TICKET-894 ("Harden entity fromJson deserialization for legacy creator keys, timestamps, and nested maps"—the follow-up ticket split out of TICKET-482) and ran an A/B test in the exact same IDE with the exact same rules and tools: first with open-weight GPT-OSS 120B (Medium) for 791 steps (67 minutes) until I pulled the plug, and then with Gemini 4 (FT-222), which finished the ticket cleanly with 0 nudges.

Here is the scorecard from that 791-step crash test:

What Happened on TICKET-894 Frontier Model (Gemini 4) Open-Weight Test (GPT-OSS 120B) Why GPT-OSS 120B Failed
/etc/init.d State Files (<brain>/state/*.md) 100% (00..99 written) 0 files created Ignored SKILL.md and Turn-1 rules completely.
fork() Subagents Spawned (SCAR-PROC-95) 100% (Archaeologist, TDD, Critic) 0 subagents forked Dumped all 104 shell commands and 52 file reads into the main window.
Context Lobotomies (CHECKPOINT) 0 6 compactions (Steps 119..772) Flooded its own window, then woke up with total amnesia 6 times.
Botched Tool Calls (ERROR_MESSAGE) 0 (0.0%) 50 errors (13.6% of turns) Printed raw JSON tool syntax inside its <thinking> block with empty output.
Searching Google for Private Local Code 0 13 calls (search_web) Used Google Web Search to look for private Dart classes inside our own repo!
Simultaneous Background git commit Jobs 1 (waited cleanly) 6 running at once Set WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0 on git commit, then ran rm -f .git/index.lock while commits were still alive!
Outcome Merged (0 nudges) Aborted at Step 791 (18 nudges) Failed to finish any of the 4 ticket items.

Two scenes from GPT-OSS 120B's flight recorder tell the whole story:

  • Finding ParseLegacy, Getting Lobotomized, and Searching Google for It (Steps 90–213): At Step 91 (after I nudged it to stop searching Google and run rg locally), GPT-OSS 120B found ParseLegacy in packages/helpers/lib/src/json/json.dart and noted in its thoughts that ParseLegacy already handled int and map. Because it never wrote 15_archaeology_receipt.md to disk, Compaction #1 hit at Step 119 and wiped that file path from its memory. Waking up with no /etc/init.d files on disk, GPT-OSS 120B called Google Web Search (search_web(query: "ParseLegacy")) twice (Steps 192 & 196), announced "I'm still not seeing the ParseLegacy implementation in this repository", and spent the next 580 steps inventing a brand-new duplicate ParseLegacyAuth class from scratch!
  • Zero-Millisecond git commit Fork-Bombing (Steps 480–710): On 7 of its 10 git commit calls, GPT-OSS 120B passed WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0—backgrounding git commit #1 after 0 milliseconds while it still held .git/index.lock. On the next turn, it fired git commit #2, hit Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists, ran rm -f .git/index.lock while git commit #1 was still running, and launched five more background git commit jobs all corrupting the same Git index at once!

The Four "Driver's License" Checks for Any Autonomous Model

Why can Gemini 4 (Low) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 cruise through the Makefile workflow with zero repeat regressions, while GPT-OSS 120B drove straight into a ditch?

Because an external checklist and dashboard can replace deep puzzle-solving (Low vs. High thinking), but they cannot help a driver who can't read the steering wheel. Before any model can use a Makefile and /etc/init.d harness, it must pass four basic "driver's license" checks:

  1. Turn-1 Rule Obedience: Does it actually open SKILL.md and create 00_governance.md on Turn 1 before editing code?
  2. Clean Tool Calling: Can it invoke tools cleanly without dumping raw JSON inside its <thinking> thoughts?
  3. Basic Tool Sense: Does it know to search local files with rg instead of Google Web Search, and to wait for git commit instead of backgrounding it after 0ms?

When you put the Harvard study's 718-company bottleneck next to these 2,677 steps of live production telemetry (926 steps across 5 tickets + 960 steps on FT-184 + 791 steps on GPT-OSS 120B), the takeaway is crystal clear:

Making it legal—and mandatory—for an Archaeologist subagent to stamp a bad ticket CONTRADICTED (TICKET-553) and for a local Adversarial Critic to catch subtle framework bugs (TICKET-482) before git commit is how you keep junk out of your human reviewers' queues.

articles.title: One Dev, Four Specialists: My Agent Team for OpenCode 🧑‍💻
articles.description: Overview   Hey everyone 👋  For a long time my OpenCode workflow was one agent, one giant...
articles.body_html:
Overview

Hey everyone 👋

For a long time my OpenCode workflow was one agent, one giant conversation, and me asking it to code, then review, then fix the SEO, then update the docs. It works, but the context gets messy, and the agent that just wrote the code is the worst one to judge it.

So I rebuilt the setup as a small team: one primary agent that builds, and four subagents it delegates to. Each one has its own role, its own boundaries and its own dedicated skill. Every agent is a single markdown file, so the whole thing is easy to read, tweak and version.

Let's dive in! 🤙

The Team 👥

web-developer is the primary agent, a senior web dev for Astro, Vue, TypeScript, Vite, Bulma and Tailwind. It's the one I talk to, and it owns the implementation.

Then four subagents, all launched by the web-developer:

ux-ui-expert designs and reviews UI, UX and graphics, always respecting the project's design system.

code-reviewer reviews changes, a feature or the whole codebase, and reports issues by severity.

seo-expert audits on-page, technical and content SEO.

documentation-updater keeps README, changelog and guides in sync with the code.

The flow is natural: I describe a feature, the web-developer proposes a plan, builds it after my OK, then calls the right specialists before we call it done.

The Golden Rule: Propose First, Apply After Approval ✋

This is the heart of the setup, and it's the same in every agent. Nobody edits files in the first pass. They present a concrete proposal (files to change, what changes, why) and wait for my explicit approval. Then, when they do apply something, every single write is gated by an ask permission, so I confirm it again.

The relay matters too. When a subagent proposes fixes, the web-developer passes the proposal to me instead of applying it on its own. Two checkpoints, no silent changes, and if something unexpected shows up mid-application, the instruction is to stop and report instead of improvising.

Anatomy of an Agent File 🔧

OpenCode has primary agents (the ones you talk to, switched with Tab) and subagents (specialists called by a primary agent, or by you with an @ mention). Agents live in .opencode/agents/ and the file name becomes the agent name. Here's the frontmatter of my code-reviewer, trimmed:

---
description: Expert code reviewer for the current project, proposes fixes and applies them only after approval.
mode: subagent
color: "#f59e0b"
permissions:
  # load and follow the dedicated skill
  - action: skill
    resource: code-review
    effect: allow
  # approval gate: every write asks for confirmation
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: ask
  # web access for docs and known issues
  - action: webfetch
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  # connected MCP servers, when necessary
  - action: "*_*"
    resource: "*"
    effect: allow
  # sandbox: nothing outside the workspace
  - action: external_directory
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
---

Two details I like. First, the sandbox rule goes last on purpose: for external_directory the last matching rule wins, so that deny overrides every allow above it, including the MCP one. Agents can't read or write outside the current project, not even through the terminal. Second, web access and MCP servers are always allowed, but the prompt tells the agent not to overuse them and to try project knowledge first.

Below the frontmatter comes the prompt: role, process, operating boundaries and the report format.

One Dedicated Skill Per Subagent 🎯

Each subagent has a global skill it must load first, before doing anything else:

  • code-reviewer loads code-review
  • seo-expert loads seo-audit
  • ux-ui-expert loads web-design
  • documentation-updater loads update-documentation

The split is simple. The agent file says who the agent is and what it's allowed to do. The skill holds the actual checklist and workflow, loaded on demand so it doesn't clutter the context when it isn't needed. For example, the documentation-updater follows a fixed path: establish repository context, understand the change, inspect the implementation, search for documentation drift, plan, edit, validate, review the diff.

Because the skills are global, I can reuse them across every project and improve them in one place.

How the Delegation Works 🧭

The web-developer prompt has a dedicated section for each specialist, saying exactly when to call it: code reviews, SEO audits and pre-ship checks, UI work and responsive fixes, documentation and changelog updates. It's explicit about what the specialist will bring back, too.

The reports are structured and that's what makes them useful:

code-reviewer returns findings ordered from critical to info, each with path:line, why it matters and a concrete fix. It also notes what is good, because a review that is only a list of problems isn't balanced.

seo-expert returns findings by severity grouped as on-page, technical and content, with before and after snippets, a separate list of quick wins, and the items that need input from me.

ux-ui-expert returns design proposals ranked by impact, the files to edit, asset recommendations and anything it can't decide without brand facts.

documentation-updater returns a plan first: files to modify, files to add, files to leave alone and why. It only documents what it can verify against the implementation.

And one rule I really like, shared by all of them: if a fact only I know (brand info, copy, a release version), flag it and ask, never invent it.

Why This Beats a Single Agent 💡

Fresh eyes. The agent that wrote the code isn't the one reviewing it. That alone catches more than any "now review what you just wrote" prompt.

Cleaner context. Each subagent works in its own child session, so the review reasoning doesn't pollute the building conversation.

Predictable behavior. Same approval gate, same sandbox, same reporting style, across the whole team.

The routine is built in. Review, SEO, design and docs checks are part of the setup, not something I have to remember at the end of every task.

The Downsides 😬

It's not free magic. More agents means more tokens and more waiting, so for a one line fix it's overkill and I simply stay in the web-developer. The approval flow adds clicks, and with two checkpoints it can feel heavy on small tasks, though I prefer that to surprise edits. Subagent descriptions need care too, because similar descriptions make the primary agent pick the wrong one. And a review only helps if you actually read it.

Final Thoughts 🌟

Splitting one do-everything agent into a team looked like a small change, but it changed how I work. I stopped micromanaging prompts at the end of every task, and I got a setup where nothing touches my code without a proposal and a yes from me.

If you use OpenCode, start small: one primary agent plus one reviewer with the approval gate. Once you see the difference, you'll want the rest of the team.

Happy coding! ✨

articles.title: "I'm 93% confident" is a string, not a probability
articles.description: The gap between the demo and the pipeline   In the demo, you ask the model to return a...
articles.body_html:
The gap between the demo and the pipeline

In the demo, you ask the model to return a confidence score alongside its answer. It says 0.93. You write if confidence > 0.9: auto_approve() and move on.

In production, that number is just more generated text. Nobody measured it against outcomes. It looks like a probability, it's formatted like a probability, and your code treats it like a probability. That is how false precision becomes automated risk.

A confidence score earns the word "confidence" only when it is calibrated: of all the cases where the system said ~90%, roughly 90% were actually correct. Until you've checked that on your own data, the number is decoration.

Failure mode 1: the threshold that was never tested

Illustrative scenario: a team routes invoice classification through an LLM and auto-processes anything above 0.9. On their eval set, accuracy is 94%. Looks great.

What they never measured is accuracy within the >0.9 bucket. When someone finally slices it, the high-confidence bucket is barely better than the low-confidence one. The model emits 0.9+ on almost everything. The threshold wasn't filtering anything; it was a rubber stamp with a decimal point.

Failure mode 2: one accuracy number hiding two systems

If your system can defer (hand off to a human, ask for clarification, fall back to a rule), then you're not evaluating one number. You're evaluating a trade-off:

  • Coverage: how often does the system answer instead of deferring?
  • Selective accuracy: when it answers, how often is it right?

Push the threshold up and coverage drops while selective accuracy (hopefully) rises. Whether it actually rises is the whole question. Here's the minimal version of measuring it:

import numpy as np

def coverage_accuracy_curve(conf, correct, thresholds):
    conf, correct = np.asarray(conf), np.asarray(correct)
    rows = []
    for t in thresholds:
        answered = conf >= t
        coverage = answered.mean()
        sel_acc = correct[answered].mean() if answered.any() else float("nan")
        rows.append((t, round(coverage, 3), round(sel_acc, 3)))
    return rows

def calibration_bins(conf, correct, n_bins=10):
    conf, correct = np.asarray(conf), np.asarray(correct)
    edges = np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (conf >= lo) & (conf < hi)
        if m.any():
            print(f"[{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f})  n={m.sum():4d}  "
                  f"stated={conf[m].mean():.2f}  actual={correct[m].mean():.2f}")

If "stated" and "actual" drift apart in the bins you care about, your threshold is lying to you.

Failure mode 3: the global threshold

Even a calibrated score can be calibrated on average and miscalibrated everywhere that matters. Illustrative scenario: overall, the 0.9 bucket is 91% correct. Split by language and the English tickets sit at 95% while the Greek and German ones sit far lower. Split by input quality and the clean PDFs are fine while the scanned, OCR'd ones fall apart.

One threshold across all of that averages away exactly the failures you built the deferral path to catch. Run the same curve per slice:

for slice_name, idx in slices.items():   # e.g. by task type, language, source quality
    print(slice_name, coverage_accuracy_curve(conf[idx], correct[idx], [0.7, 0.8, 0.9]))

If the curves differ meaningfully, you need per-slice thresholds, or you need to stop trusting the score for that slice at all.

Failure mode 4: verbalized vs. measured confidence

Asking the model "how sure are you?" and reading token log-probs are different signals, and neither is calibrated by default. Self-reported numbers in particular tend to cluster on round, reassuring values. Treat any source of confidence (verbal, log-prob, ensemble agreement, a separate verifier) as a hypothesis to test, not a fact to consume.

The reframe

Confidence isn't a model property. It's a system property you have to measure. The real question isn't "does the model feel sure?" It's "is the system's decision to proceed reliable for this task, in this context, on this kind of input?"

Practical checklist

  1. Log every decision with its confidence, the slice metadata, and the eventual ground truth.
  2. Plot coverage vs. selective accuracy, globally and per slice.
  3. Check calibration bins in the range where your threshold actually sits.
  4. Re-run it when the model, prompt, or input distribution changes. Calibration doesn't survive a model swap.

How are you deciding when your LLM pipeline is allowed to act without a human? Is anyone here actually running per-slice thresholds in production, or is everyone on a single global cutoff?

articles.title: PHP vulnerability PHP2Shell: what the October 21 emergency release fixed and what is still disputed
articles.description: PHP2Shell is two critical PHP remote code execution flaws fixed on October 21, 2026. A plain-language look at the bugs, the leaked embargo, who reports exploitation, and
articles.body_html:
The PHP vulnerability called PHP2Shell is two critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, fixed in an emergency release on October 21, 2026. PHP runs an estimated 70% of websites according to the Guardian and Wiz, so the question for a developer is simple: which copies of PHP do you run, and are they patched? The better story is how the bug waited two years for a decision, how the embargo leaked, and why sources disagree about exploitation.

TL;DR

  • PHP2Shell covers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0 by the PHP team. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 got source patches only.
  • The flaws sit in memory and error handling, which nearly every request touches. On Apache with mod_php the first one can run before any application code, so a login page cannot stop it.
  • A PHP core developer saw the first signs in a 2024 audit. Competing fixes had trade-offs and a consensus-based security team struggled to choose. The PHP Foundation calls the delay a structural failure.
  • Amazon logged an attempt on October 17, four days before the patch. CISA had not observed exploitation at publication, and several analysts say many public exploit scripts do not work. Patch anyway.
  • The same day GitLab shipped a critical patch release, and a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion.

What is the PHP vulnerability called PHP2Shell?

PHP2Shell is the nickname for two flaws that let an unauthenticated stranger run code on a server through ordinary web requests. The official advisories are GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w for CVE-2026-109618, titled "RCE via OOM corruption", and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp for CVE-2026-109619, titled "RCE via stale global state". The earliest affected code path dates to PHP 5.4.0.

PHP is a scripting language that builds web pages on the server just before they reach the visitor. It is over thirty years old, and WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki are written in it. The Guardian describes the nonprofit PHP Foundation as having about thirteen full-time and part-time engineers, which matters for the rest of the story.

Wiz points out that the problem sits in PHP itself, below whatever application runs on top. Even a hello world script on an affected version is exposed, so the WordPress, Drupal and Joomla demonstrations are examples.

How does PHP remote code execution work here, in plain words?

No exploit steps appear here. The mechanism is explained at the level the PHP advisories use.

The first flaw starts with memory limits. Every PHP request gets a memory budget. If a request hits that limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP exits the current work in a hurry and can leave the request memory half built. The cleanup step may later read or branch on that half-built data. On Apache with mod_php the cleanup runs even when request startup failed, entirely before application code begins. PHP-FPM removes the child when startup fails, which blocks that path, although the advisory says FPM is still susceptible through other routes.

The second flaw is a leftover. A worker keeps some global state between requests, such as error, session and object state. A fatal error can abandon an operation before it resets that state, so the worker holds a pointer to memory that belonged to the previous request. A later request handled by the same worker can then use that stale pointer before normal initialization replaces it.

The fix removes PHP's emergency exit for running out of memory. Instead of bailing out of the middle of a request, PHP now schedules a graceful stop at the next safe point, and it only hard-stops past a second, higher threshold. Both advisories say updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. Partial measures exist, and PHP's team says they only reduce exposure.

Why did a known PHP memory bug wait two years?

The PHP Foundation's post-mortem is unusually frank. In 2024 PHP had its first external security audit in years, funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency and carried out by Quarkslab. While fixing one reported issue, a Foundation-contracted core developer found the first signs of the out-of-memory problem. A potential exploit was theorized, but no concrete vector was found and other issues with clear impact took priority.

Fixing it was hard. Each competing approach had a cost: broken backward compatibility, new denial-of-service risk, or changes to many third-party extensions. The team decides by consensus and, in the Foundation's words, "struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice." Work stalled and restarted for months. The Foundation says plainly that the delay was a structural failure caused by the decision process and a lack of resources, and that the team is moving to majority decisions and bringing leadership in sooner on hard trade-offs.

Who found PHP2Shell, and did AI find it?

In August, finders arrived within days. Calif began a PHP audit on July 30 under OpenAI's Patch the Planet program, and researcher Ryan Austin reported the first bug on August 11. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause the same day, and Wiz, using Wiz Atlas, Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, found and reported variants on August 24.

How much the models mattered is contested. OpenAI said frontier AI was key. Calif's own write-up says no special harness or non-public model was used in the initial discovery, and credits a theory about where PHP's old bugs hide. Chainguard's CEO told The Register his team independently found the same bugs on a Friday night with a basic prompt asking for bad vulnerabilities in PHP. The common thread is that finding this class of bug got much cheaper, and a months-long embargo now has to survive that.

How did the PHP2Shell embargo leak?

The coordinated release was set for October 22 at 14:00 UTC. According to the Foundation, on Tuesday October 20 around 15:00 UTC the two CVE IDs began circulating on forums and social media with a wrong release time and a wrong score of 10.0. The Hacker News post that carried them reached 282 points. PHP published a pre-announcement at 19:30 UTC and moved the release forward a day.

Around 20:00 UTC Calif mistakenly published a video of its proof of concept, and copies circulated after it was deleted. On Wednesday at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the release, Chainguard published built images containing the fix. The Foundation says any attacker could study the fix in binary form while everyone else waited. A patch is also a diff, and attackers read diffs.

Chainguard's CEO says the company did not leak, that people were already being hit, and that it made the call to ship the fixes. The timeline itself is not in dispute.

Is PHP2Shell being exploited? What the sources say

  • Amazon Threat Intelligence logged an exploitation attempt on a honeypot on October 17 and more attempts on October 21 from different infrastructure. It says it is unclear whether those attempts would have worked on real systems, and later said PHP2Shell is broadly exploited.
  • watchTowr reported exploitation in the wild through its honeypot network. Cloudflare's CEO said it saw thousands of attempts in the ten hours before the announcement and millions by Thursday morning.
  • CISA said it had not observed exploitation as of publication. The PHP team said it identified no functional exploit at release.
  • watchTowr also says many exploit scripts flying around crash or do nothing. VulnCheck, as relayed by Tanium, found code execution works in some setups and that none of the public ones beat memory randomization on standard x86-64. Researcher Elias Taylor argues the bug is nowhere near as easy as Log4Shell, and still says patch.

An attempt is only a knock on the door. Amazon's advice is to investigate from at least October 17.

Which PHP versions get a PHP security update?

Fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. For 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 the PHP project published minimal source patches only. Older versions get nothing from the PHP project, and distributions may backport fixes, so ask your vendor. PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

Governments did not wait. The NSA told organizations that could not patch to take PHP systems offline, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice. The Guardian reports that Dutch sites including the national digital identity service, a Paris police site and several UK council sites went offline, and that Wikimedia took systems down as a precaution. Palo Alto Networks counted more than 22 million exposed instances.

What to do about PHP2Shell tonight

CISA's guidance is a good checklist: inventory every system that runs PHP, including copies inside other software, patch internet-facing systems first, and take PHP systems offline if you cannot update. Restart the workers after updating. Review logs back to October 17 for memory-limit errors and PHP workers launching shells.

This is the same lesson as the previous Daily Diff episode on eMudhra: a fix existing is not the same as the running process having it.

Two other stories from the same day

GitLab shipped critical patch releases, led by 19.5.1, on October 21. Its advisory describes an integer overflow in the regular expression compiler that could let an unauthenticated user execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. It is CVE-2026-110264 with a CVSS 3.1 score of 10.0, affecting versions back to 7.0. GitLab.com is already patched; self-managed installations need the update.

In New Mexico, a judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties in the state's Cambridge Analytica case, according to CNBC. The jury counted more than 43 million violations at up to $5,000 each, and the filing shows $219.5 billion awarded before it was reduced to $25 billion. Meta's chief legal officer said the company is confident it will prevail on appeal. It is a court order that Meta is appealing.

Verdict: SHIP IT

I would ship the PHP update tonight. The new version number is the only complete fix, the exploitation picture is disputed but real attempts exist, and the cost of an unneeded restart is small compared with a compromised server.

FAQ

Is PHP2Shell a zero-day?
Amazon logged an attempt four days before the fix, but the sources do not establish that any attempt succeeded. Call it a critical flaw with disputed exploitation.

Do WAF rules or config changes replace patching?
No. PHP, Amazon and the other vendors say updating is the only complete fix. Edge rules and settings such as limiting upload size reduce some paths.

What if I run an unsupported PHP version?
Ask your distribution for a backport, apply PHP's source patches for 7.4, 8.0 or 8.1 if you build from source, or plan a move to a supported version.

  • Wiz Research: PHP2Shell
  • Amazon Threat Intelligence: MadPot
